full_judgment:
Jahangir Hossain, J: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the Judgment and deciee dated the 6th day of July, 2006 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree (FA) No. 561 of 1991 allowing the appeal. 

2. The relevant facts for disposal of the instant civil appeal, in brief, are that the appellant, as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 48 of 1985 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Feni, praying for declaration that 4 (four) deeds executed on 21-4-1982 and registered on 18-8-1982 are forged, fraudulent, inoperative, without consideration and ante-dated etc. The case of the appellant is that 162 decimels of land originally belonged to ATM Mujibul Huq Mia [defendant No.1] and his brother-Nurul Huq. On 23-4-1982, defendant No.1 transferred his share equivalent to 81 decimals of land to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 26,000 [twenty six thousand only) that thereby the right, title and interest of defendant No.1 extinguished in the scheduled property. Subsequently, the plaintiff came to know that defendant No.1 collusively executed ante-dated 4 [four] saf-kabala deeds (Deed Nos. 5849-5852] registered on 18-8-1982 in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5 showing the date of execution on 21-4-1982 in respect of 150 decimals of land which he had no power to transfer. The plaintiff further came to learn that one Shamsul Huq purchased 3(three) stamps on 29-3-1982 bearing serial Nos. 32373, 32374 and 32375 from Cumilla Treasury, value of each of them is Taka 1,500 by which defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 5 created kabala in their names. The plaintiff on 6-10-1982 having searched in Cumilla Treasury came to know that originally, these stamps were purchased by one Lucki Ahmed, value of each of them is Taka 600. One Joynal Abedin was shown as purchaser of stamp bearing serial No.12327 dated 15-4-1982 at consideration of Taka 1,000 which was used in the kabala of defendant No. 4, but 15-4-1982 was the public holiday and no stamp was sold on that day. On search in Noakhali Treasury, it is also known that the stamp bearing serial No.12327 dated 5-8-1982 was issued in favour of one Abdul Khaleque. There is no mention of any name of the defendants in purchasing and selling of the stamps. Without purchasing from Feni Treasury, the stamps were purchased from Noakhali and Cumilla Treasury in different person's names. In fact, the stamps used in kabalas by the defendants are not purchased from Noakhali or Cumilla Treasury. The defendants in collusion with each other having :::oilected unsold stamps created the disputed deeds. The defendants never possessed the suit land in pursuance of the disputed deeds. 

3. Furthermore, the plaintiff having learned about defrauding, forgery and ante-dated deeds on 27-8-1982 at first, filed CR No. 768 of 1982 in the Court of Feni Sub-Division under section 420/465 of the Penal Code collecting the certified copy of the deeds and when the talabana notice was served upon the defendants, they preferred Criminal Miscellaneous Revision Case No. 60 of 1982 in the District Judge Adalat. Having heard both the sides, this revision case was dismissed on 1-3-1983. Against the said dismissal order, the defendants preferred Criminal Revision Case No.155 of 1983 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division having heard both the sides discharged the Rule on 29-6-1983. Subsequently, after the establishment of the Upazila Adalat, the aforesaid case was transferred to Dagan Bhuiyan Upazila, the plaintiff filed Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 305 of 1984 before the District Judge Court and the learned District Judge dismissed the case and sent the case to lower Court for fresh hearing. The case was heard and testimony was recorded and a date was fixed for judgment. But the learned Magistrate without pronouncing the judgment fixed the case for framing charge and in absence of the plaintiff side, the Magistrate acquitted the defendants. Even though the plaintiff is entitled to get relief in the higher Court against the order of the learned Magistrate, he instituted the civil suit against the fraudulent, forged. infructuous and ante-dated deeds having no consideration. 

4. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statements denying material allegation of the plaint contending, inter alia, that he sold 11 decimals of land to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 10,000 but the plaintiff collusively replaced 11 consideration decimals of Taka by 81 decimals 26.000 instead of at a Taka 
10,000. When the matter was brought to light, he refused to register sale deeds in favour of the plaintiff. But subsequently, the matter was resolved at the intervention of the then VP Joynal Abedin, MP to the effect that the plaintiff would return 70 decimals of land to defendant No.1. Thereafter, both the parties kept their respective deeds with him (VP Joynal Abedin), subsequently, he lost those deeds. 

5. Defendant Nos. 2-5 also contested the suit by filing a joint written statements contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Nirmal Kumar Shil and others through chain of succession from the recorded tenants who transferred the same to defendant Nos. 2-5 by 6 (six) registered deeds dated 28-4-1989 at a consideration of Taka 60,000. Subsequently, when it has brought to the notice of them that the khatian in respect of the suit land was prepared in the name of defendant No.1 and his brother-Nurul Huq, then again they purchased the suit land from defendant No.1 who got 162 decimals of land by amicable arrangement with his brother. No fraud was practiced for execution and registration of deeds, the stamps were collected by Joynal Abedin, on 15-4-1982 on behalf of them and the remaining facts are same as stated by defendant No.1 in his written statements. 

6. During trial, the plaintiff examined as many as 5(five) witnesses and defendant Nos. 2-5 also examined 5 [five] witnesses in support of their respective case. Defendant No.1 was also examined as witness. 

7. Upon hearing the parties and after considering the evidence and relevant materials on record, the learned Sub-Judge [now Joint District Judge), Feni, on 25-9-1998 decreed Title Suit No. 48 of 1985 in part. 

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendants preferred First Appeal No. 561 of 1991 before the High Court Division and the learned Judges of the High Court Division on 6-7-2006 allowed the appeal with cost setting aside those of the trial Court. 

9. Against the impugned judgment and decree dated 6-7-2006 passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiff-appellant preferred the instant civil appeal before this Division which has arisen out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1259 of 2006. 

10. Mr. Swapan Kumar Dutta, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the stamp bearing No. 12327 dated 15-4-1982 of Deed No. 5851 was purchased from Noakhali Treasury by Joynal Abedin which, as per record of the treasury, shows that the said stamp was purchased by one Abdul on 5-8-1982 and that Khaleque 15-4-1982 declared a government holiday being the 1st day of Baishak which was corroborated by PW 4, Noakhali Treasury and that the trial staff of COUEL on scrutiny found that Number 12327 was printed in the backside of the stamp of the said deed. Number 2 is penned through and over-writings are found in the concerned stamp and that purchaser, Joynal Abedin, has not been examined as witness in the case and that the genuineness of the said deed is doubtful and Deed No. 5852 stands in the name of defendant No. 5, Mafia Khatun, and Deed No. 5850 stands in the name of defendant No. 3, Kobbat Ahmed, those stamps bearing Nos. 32373, 32374, 32375 respectively were purchased in the name of Shamsul Hogue, PW 5, a staff of Cumilla Treasury who deposed on production of stamp register to the effect that one Lucky Ahmed was the purchaser of those stamps and there is erasing mark on the stamp bearing No. 32373 and there being no explanation regarding said erasing marks and over-writings and Shamsul Hague, the alleged purchaser of those stamps, having not being examined in the case, there is serious doubt about the genuineness of those deeds of the defendants and there being explanation about the delay of 
4[four] months in registering the disputed deeds of the defendants sufficiently proved that the defendants' disputed deeds are ante-dated and accordingly, decreed the suit, but the Appellate Court without considering those findings of the trial Court erred in allowing the appeal. Having regard to the established principle of law that between two genuine sale deeds one which has been executed earlier but registered later on, will prevail over one which has been executed on a later date but registered on an earlier date and in the present case, the trial Court having found that though the disputed deeds of the defendants were executed two days earlier, those were found to be ante-dated and the plaintiff's deed being executed and registered on 23-4-1982 and being genuine, the learned Judges of the High Court Division ought to have held that the disputed deeds being ante-dated cannot prevail over the genuine deed of the plaintiff, that the defendants in order to frustrate the effectiveness of the deed of the plaintiff dated 23-4-1982 created the disputed deeds dated 21-4-1982 by ante-dating the same and, as such, the same cannot prevail over the plaintiff's deed dated 23-4-1982 and having decreed the suit in part, that the learned Judge of the trial Court found that—
"উল্লেখযোগ্য যে ৪নং বিবাদীর দলিল নং ৫৮৫১ এবং দলিলটির স্ট্যাম্প নোয়াখালী ট্রেজারী থেকে জয়নাল আবেদীন সংগ্রহ করেছেন বলে প্রকাশ আছে। বিবাদীপক্ষ থেকে এই মর্মে বলা হয়েছে যে, উক্ত জয়নাল আবেদীন ৪নং বিবাদীর পুত্র। দেখা যাচ্ছে যে, উক্ত স্ট্যাম্পটি ১,০০০.০০ টাকা মূল্যের নম্বর ১২৩২৭ এবং তারিখ ১৫-৪-১৯৮২। বাদীপক্ষ অনুসন্ধান পূর্বক জেনেছেন যে, প্রকৃত পক্ষে এ স্ট্যাম্পটি খরিদ করে ছিলেন জনৈক আব্দুল খালেক ৫-৮-১৯৮২ ইং তারিখে। দলিলে স্ট্যাম্পটি ১৫-৪-১৯৮২ ইং তারিখ উল্লেখ আছে যা সরকারী ছুটির দিন ছিল। এ বিষয়ে উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে যে, ১৫-৪-১৯৮২ ইং তারিখ নববর্ষ হিসাবে সরকারী ছুটি ছিল যা আদালতের দৃষ্টি গ্রাহ্য তথ্য। এই বিষয়ে বাদীপক্ষের ৪নং সাক্ষী নোয়াখালী ট্রেজারীর স্ট্যাফ আবুল কাশেম এতদবিষয়ে রেজিস্টার প্রদর্শন পূর্���ক বলেন যে ৫-৮-১৯৮২ ইং তারিখে উক্ত নম্বরের স্ট্যাম্পটি আব্দুল খালেকের নিকট বিক্রয় করেন। দলিল প্রমাণ ভিত্তিক এই সাক্ষীর সাক্ষ্যের গুরুত্ব অস্বীকার করা যায় না। দলিলটির পেছনে দেখা যাচ্ছে যে, স্ট্যাম্প নম্বরটি ১২৩২৭ফিত্র ৪র্থ সংখ্যায় ২ তে কাটাকাটি আছে এবং দেখা যাচ্ছে যে, ২ এর আগে ৩ ছিল। এই দলিলে স্ট্যাম্প বিষয়ক নোটে ১৫/৪ লেখা থাকলেও অপর একটি লেখার উপর লিখিত এবং তা ৭ অথবা ৮ হতে পারে বলে ধারণা করা হচ্ছে। স্ট্যাম্প খরিদ্দার হিসাবে নালিশী গ্রামের জয়নাল আবেদীন মর্মে উল্লেখ আছে যিনি জবাবের কথা মতে ৪ নং বিবাদীর পুত্র। এতদবিষয়ে জয়নাল আবেদীন কোন সাক্ষ্য প্রদান করেননি। তাই এই বিষয়ে সাক্ষ্য আইনের ১১৪ ধারা অনুসারে প্রতিকূল অনুমান করা যায়। দেখা যাচ্ছে যে, স্ট্যাম্প এর বিষয়ে হেরফের করা হয়েছে। এই দলিলটি প্রদর্শন-২(খ)। ৫৮৫২ নং দলিলের গ্রহীতা ৫নং বিবাদীনি মাফিয়া খাতুন। ৫৮৪৯ নং দলিলের গ্রহীতা ২নং বিবাদী মকবুল আহাং, ৫৮৫০নং দলিলের গ্রহিতা ৩নং বিবাদী কোব্বাদ আহাং। উপরোক্ত ৩টি দলিল যথাক্রমে কুমিল্লা ট্রেজারী থেকে প্রাপ্ত ২৯-৩-১৯৮২ ইং তারিখের ৩২৩৭৪, ৩২৩৭৩, ৩২৩৭৫ নং স্ট্যাম্প এর উপর লেখা হয়। স্ট্যাম্প খরিদ্দার হিসাবে আছে সামছুল হক। এই বিষয়ে ট্রেজারীর কর্মচারী বাদী পক্ষের ৫নং সাক্ষী রেজিস্টার প্রদান। পূর্বক প্রকাশ করেন যে, উপরোক্ত নম্বরের স্ট্যাম্প সমূহের ক্রেতা ছিলেন লাকী আহাং। তার সাক্ষ্যের গুরুত্ব উপেক্ষা করা যায় না। দেখা যাচ্ছে যে, ৩২৩৭৩ নং স্ট্যাম্পটির নম্বরে ঘষামাঝা করা হয়েছে।

11. Mr. Md. Jahangir Kabir, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 1(a)-1(h) and 2(a)-2(f) supported the impugned judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division. 

12. Heard the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and the relevant materials along with other connected papers on record. 

13. Upon perusal of the judgment of the High Court Division it appears that it was justified in taking the stance that the plaintiff's declaratory suit against the disputed deeds was maintainable. In the case of Sufia Khanain Chowdhury vs Faizun Nesa Chowdhury, reported in 39 DLR (AD) 46, it was held that section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 does not specifically provide for declaration of nullity of any written instrument; nevertheless, a decree for nullity of any instrument comes under this section in view of the general provision therein as to declaration of any legal character as expressed in the words "any person entitled to any legal character". If, by an instrument a person's right and title is clouded or threatened, he may seek a declaration under this section to the effect that by the instrument his right and title has not been affected or that any other person who denies his title or claims title in himself has not acquired any right or title thereby. 

14. The stance taken by the High Court Division regarding the valuation of the suit and Court fees appears to be justified since in a suit for pure declaration, fixed Court-fee has to be paid as per section 7 (iv) read with Article 12 (111) Schedule-II of the Court-fees Act, 1870. In suits for declaratory decrees, pure and simple and those in which it is impossible to estimate at a money value the subject-matter in dispute falling under Article 17, Schedule 2, the amount of fees payable is fixed [Kumudini Welfare' Trust vs Pakistan, 11 DLR 571.
 
15. In the instant case the dispute between the parties mainly rests on the point as to whether the deed executed by defendant No.1 in favour of the plainfiff vide deed No. 4668 dated 23-4-1982 executed and registered on the same date) would get priority over the disputed deeds allegedly executed by defendant No.1 on 21-4-82 in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5 which were registered on 18-8-1982 vide deed Nos. 5849, 5850. 5851 and 5852 of 18-8-1982. Priority of deed is determined by section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 read with section 47 of the Registration Act, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act states that where a person purports to create by transfer at different times rights in or over the same immovable property, and such rights cannot all exist or be exercised to their full extent together, each later created right shall, in the absence of a special contract or reservation binding the earlier transferees, be subject to the rights previously created. Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act recognizes the broader principle that later created right shall be subject to the rights previously created. But a document may be registered later from the date of execution which may create controversy as to the point of time regarding the creation of right. In order to remove such controversy there is provision in section 47 of the Act to the effect that a registered document shall operate not from the date of registration but from the date of its execution. It is very difficult to manipulate the date of registration since registration of document essentially entails keeping records of the same in the Public Office. Execution of document being in the hands of the parties. there may be collusion between the parties to manipulate the date of execution so as to deprive any holder of any deed executed previously. So, question may arise regarding the date of execution of deed and priority of transfer. The date of execution of deed being a question of fact needs to be determined appreciating the evidence on record. 

16. Priority of transfer necessarily involves the question whether the defendant No. 1 had title to the disputed 162 decimals of land. Defendant Nos. 2-5 claimed that the disputed land beloneed to Nirmal Kumar Singh and others through chain of succession from the recorded tenants and they transferred the same to defendant Nos. 2-5 by 6 kabala deeds but record was not prepared in the name of Nirmal Kumar Singh and others by mistake. Rather, SA record-of-rights of the disputed property was prepared in the name of defendant No.1 and his brother Nurul Hague. Nurul Haque by compromise transferred his portion to defendant No.l. Defendant Nos. 2-5 claims that though defendant No.1 and his brother did not have title over the suit land, they purchased the disputed land from defendant No.1 to avoid complexity. This stance of defendant Nos. 2-5 is not acceptable since they have purchased the disputed property acknowledging the title of defendant No.1 over the suit property, they are barred by estoppel under section 115 of the Evidence Act, 1872 to raise any objection with respect to the previous title of defendant No.1 over the suit land. In this case plaintiff raised the objection with respect to title of defendant No.1 over the disputed 162 decimals of land. The plaintiff is the vendee of the deed No.4668 dated 23-4-1982 and its schedule has a recital to the effect that defendant No.1 has title over the disputed 162 decimals of land. Therefore, plaintiff is also barred by estoppels under section 115 of the Evidence Act, 1872 to raise any objection about the previous title of defendant No.1 over the disputed 162 decimals of land. 

17. Defendant No.1 claims that he stipulated with the plaintiff to transfer 11 decimals of land vide deed No. 4668 dated 23-4-1982 at a consideration of Taka 10,000 but the plaintiff due to enmity wrote 81 decimals of land in place of l 1 decimals of land and consideration money was also written as Taka 26,000 instead of Taka 10,000. When he came to know this fact. he declined to register the deed in favour of the plaintiff. Through the intervention of different persons he registered the deed on condition of re-conveyance of 70 decimals of land in favour of him by the plaintiff. The plaintiff executed a deed of re-conveyance in favour of defendant No.1 in respect of 70 decimals of land. There were numerous cases among the parties and therefore, there was arbitration in presence of Zainal Abedin, MP. They submitted their documents to Zainal Abedin, MP who later on disclosed that he (Zainal Abedin) lost the deed of re-conveyance. The plaintiff denied these allegations of defendant No.1 and categorically stated that there was clear stipulation to transfer 81 decimals of land at a consideration of Taka 26.000 and accordingly deed was executed and registered and he never executed any deed of re-conveyance in favour of defendant No.1 and no arbitration took place regarding this matter. The burden of proof regarding writing 81 decimals of land in place of 11 decimals of land in the deed No. 4668 dated 23-4-1982 and regarding execution of the deed of re-conveyance was with defendant No.1, there being presumption of correctness of a registered document under section 114 illustration (e) of the Evidence Act, 1872. Defendant No. 1 did not mention the names of the persons through whose intervention it was settled that the plaintiff would re-convey 70 decimals of land in his favour. Moreover, man of ordinary prudence would not allow the deed to be registered in the above-mentioned circumstances without correcting the same in respect of quantity of the property to be transferred. Defendant No.1 could not produce any convincing evidence, discharge hia burden oral of or proof documentary, for which allegations cannot be said to have been proved. 

18. In the instant case, the appellant-plaintiff raised the point that defendant No.1 collusively executed the aforesaid disputed deeds in respect of 150 decimals of land in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5 showing date of execution on 21-4-1982 to deprive him of the rights over property which he acquired by deed No. 4668 dated 23-4-1982. The burden of proof reearding the collusion in execution of the disputed deeds primarily lies on the plaintiff as per section 101 of the Evidence Act, 1872. 

19. Let us consider whether the plaintiff has been able to discharge his burden of proof. Plaintiff categorically deposed that stamp Nos. 32373, 32374 and 32375 dated 29-3-82 of the deeds in the names of vendee/defendant Nos.2, 3, 5 were shown to be bought from Cumilla treasury in the name of Shamsul Hague but actually those stamps were sold in the name of one Lucky Ahmed. He further deposed that stamp No. 12327/6 dated 15-4-82 of the deed in the name of defendant No.4 was shown to be bought from Noakhali treasury but that day was a public holiday on the occasion of Bangla New year. He further deposed that the said stamp was actually sold to one Abdul Khaleque of Durgapur on 5-8-82. PW 1 submitted copy of the searching slip supplied from Cumilla treasury which has been marked as Exhibit No.2 (Gha). PW 1 also submitted photocopy of the searching slip supplied from Noakhali treasury, the original being submitted in the criminal case. PW 2 deposed that he was present at the time of registration of 81 decimals of land at a consideration of Taka 26,000 in favour of the plaintiff and he identified the vendor of the deed. PW 2 also proved his signature cf identification. Defendant No. 1 or defendant Nos. 2-5 could not bring any inconsistency by cross-examining him. Official witness PW 4 and PW 5 deposed in favour of the plaintiff by producing the respective registers of the sold stamps and they corroborated the testimony of PW 1 in toto. Defendant Nos. 2-5 could not bring any inconsistency by cross-examining PW 1, PW 4 and PW 5. Though there is no mandatory provision in the Stamp Act, 1899 or in the Rules framed thereunder. as to in whose name stamp has to be bought, a person is not entitled to use the stamp no and the name of the buyer of any already sold stamp in another stamp. In this case using the stamp Nos. issued in the names of other persons. overwriting on the stamp No. and date of the stamp No., rubbing the stamp No. and showing the buying of one stamp at government holiday raises serious doubt about the date of execution of the disputed deeds in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5. One disputed stamp purchaser Joynal Abedin was the son of defendant No.4 as per written statement. Defendant Nos. 2-5 could not produce Joynal Abedin and Shamsul Hag namely the persons in whose name those disputed stamps were bought to refute the allegations put forwarded by the plaintiff without offering any explanation for which the Court may draw adverse presumption against the defendant Nos. 2-5 under section 114 illustration(g) of the Evidence Act, 1872. It is the duty of the party to lead the best evidence in its possession which could throw light on the issue in controversy and in case such a material evidence is withheld, the Court may draw adverse inference under section 114 illustration(g) of the Evidence Act, 1872 notwithstanding that the onus of proof did not lie on such party and it was not called upon to produce the said evidence [Mussauddin Ahmed vs State of Assam, (2009) 14 SCC 541]. No witness was produced to prove the execution of the disputed deeds in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5. The vendor of the disputed deeds in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5 namely defendant No.1 during cross-examination by the plaintiff deposed, “ বিবাদীদের প্রাপ্ত কবলা কোন তারিখ সম্পাদন হয়েছে তারিখ মনে নাই।” This portion of the deposition of defendant No.1 also raises doubt about the date of execution of the disputed deeds in favor of defendant Nos. 2-5. In the instant case there is no explanation as to why the aforesaid disputed deeds were not registered for about 4 months and witnesses produced in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5 did not depose as to why there was 4 months delay to register the disputed deeds. It appears that the plaintiff by producing the evidence, oral and documentary, has successfully discharged his burden of proof. Defendant Nos. 2-5 failed to discharge the burden of proof which shifted to them. 

20. The High Court Division literally interpreted section 47 of the Act, 1908 but failed to perceive the spirit of it. The High Court Division being Constitutional Court was under an obligation interpret section 47 of the Act in its right perspective. Construction of a statutory provision should be agreeable to justice and reason. An intention to produce an unreasonable result is not to be imputed to a statute if there is some other construction available (Artemiou vs Procopiou (1966) 1 QB 878, per Danckwerts LJ at P 888, Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, twelfth edition by P St J Langan, page 1991. Where to apply the words literally would "defeat the obvious intention of the legislation and produce a wholly unreasonable result" we must do some violence to the words" and so achieve that obvious intention and produce & rational construction (Luke vs 112C (1963) AC 557, per Lord Reid at P 577, Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, twelfth edition by P St J Langan, page 199] For a deed to operate from the date of its execution, there should be proper execution of the same and there should not be any well founded objection to the effect that there was collusion between the parties regarding fixing previous date of execution of the deed to deprive any previous deed holder. Otherwise, the spirit of section 47 of the Act would be frustrated. Any deed the date of execution of which is highly doubtful does not seem to transfer title to the property by the mere registration of the same. In the case of Ranzalinga Muladi vs Ayyadorai Nainar another reported in 28 1LR (1905) page 124, it was held that it cannot be laid down as a general rule that mere registration of an instrument without reference to other circumstances operates to transfer the property. 

21. In the case of Ainaddin Ahmed and others vs Samaddi Hajari and others reported in 7 DER page 443, it was held that "the case here is that the document was collusively created to defeat the title of the defendants by ante-dating the same to a date prior to the date of the execution and registration of the defendants' document. In a case of this kind, I do not think that it can be said that mere registration has the effect of transferring title." 

22. In view of the abovementioned circumstances, the trial Court came to the conclusion that disputed deeds were ante-dated to deprive the plaintiff of his legitimate rights over the disputed property. Conclusion of the trial Court appears to be reasonable under section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872 since this section enunciates that the Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business, in their relation to the facts of the particular case. The High Court Division reversed the decision of the trial Court without adverting to its finding or without reversing the aforesaid specific findings of the trial Court. In the case of Gola Bewa vs Md. Abdur Rashid, reported in 4 MLR (AD) 420, the Appellate Division upheld the judgment of the High Court Division when the High Court Division set-aside the judgment of the Appellate Court taking the view that the Appellate Court did not advert to the reasoning of the trial Court or reverse the material findings of the said Court in setting aside the judgment of the trial Court. In the case of Musanunat Mohsena Khatun vs MA Habib Knitting Mills represented by its proprietor Sheikh Amjad Hassan,. reported in 27 BLD (AD) 1997 page No. 47. the Appellate Division set-aside the judgment of the High Court Division when it did not at all reverse finding of fact in reversing the decree of the trial Court. In the case of Ranfit Sarkar vs Sukhendu Bikash, reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 58 :2 BLC (AD) 100. The Appellate Division held that where the appellate Court failed to advert to the reasonings of the trial Court and also did not reverse the findings of the trial Court, the judgment of the Appellate Court is not sustainable in law. 

23. In the case in hand, the trial Court did not declare the disputed deeds ante-dated for all purposes rather it declared those deeds ante-dated vis-a-vis deed No. 4668 dated 23-4-1982 of the plaintiff which appears to be based on reason to ensure justice. 

24. Civil cases are decided on the basis preponderance of evidence while in a criminal case the entire burden lies on the prosecution and proof beyond reasonable doubt has to be given (Vishnu Dutt Sharma vs Daya Sapra 13 SCC (2009) page 7291. In the instant case, the preponderance of probability regarding the ante-dating of the disputed deeds is clearly in favour of the plaintiff. 

25. In view of the facts, circumstances and propositions of law discussed above, we are of the view that the High Court Division was not justified in interfering with the well-reasoned judgment of the trial Court. 

26. Therefore, we find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant and accordingly the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. 

Therefore, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division is set-aside. 

End.

caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 143 of 2025 with Civil Rule No. 609(FM) of 2024.
lawyer:
Md. Anisul Hassan, Advocate—For the Plaintiff= Appellant. 
Mahmud Hasan, DAG with Md. Solaiman Hossen, AAG with Mohammad Kutub Uddin (Tushar), AAG with Tashrifa Sultana Jali, AAG and Asma Hosen, AAG—For the Respondent Nos. 1 and 2. 
Muhammad Anisuzzaman, Advocate—For the Respondent No. 3.
parties:
Tie Associates Limited ------- For the Plaintiff-Appellant
VS
Bangladesh Bank and others ------ For the Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Nazrul Islam Talukder, J: This first miscellaneous appeal has been preferred by the plaintiff-appellant challenging impugned Order No. 3 dated 14-10-2024 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 5th court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 557 of 2024 rejecting the application for temporary injunction filed by the plaintiff-appellant under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. 

2. The brief facts of the plaint of the suit are as follows:—
The plaintiff-appellant is a private limited company duly incorporated and registered under the Companies Act, 1994 involved in petroleum business and since its incorporation the company is doing business with good reputation. 

3. The plaintiff-appellant filed Title Suit No.557 of 2024 before the learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka against the defendant-respondents praying for, amongst others, the following reliefs:—
(a) Pass a decree of declaration that the publication/reporting/inclusion and showing of the names of the plaintiff company and its directors in the report of Credit Information Bureau (CIB) of Bangladesh Bank as borrower defaulter in connection with the loan facilities provided by the IFIC Bank PLC, Principal Branch i.e. defendant Nos. 3 and 4, is illegal, collusive, malafide and without lawful effect and not binding upon the plaintiff. 

4. During pendency of the suit, the plaintiff filed an application for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and after hearing the aforesaid application, the learned Judge of the court below was pleased to reject the application for temporary injunction of the plaintiff vide order dated 14-10-2024. 

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order No.3 dated 14-10-2024 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 557 of 2024 rejecting the application for temporary injunction filed by the plaintiff-appellant uncle". Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the plaintiff-appellant preferred this first miscellaneous appeal before this court. 

6. When the matter is taken up for hearing, none appears for the plaintiff-appellant to press the appeal and the Rule. 

7. At the very outset, Mr. Muhammad Anisuzzaman, the learned Advocate appearing for the Respondent No.3, submits that the Respondent Nos. 3 and 4 were under a legal obligation to send the list of debtors in default to Bangladesh Bank under section 27KaKa of the Bank Company Act, 1991 and thereby they sent the name of the plaintiff-appellant into CIB as defaulters in compliance with the same; according to Chapter IV (Article 42-48) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972, Bangladesh Bank is only authorized to collect and furnish credit information of the account holders, Bangladesh Bank, on the basis of the lending Bank or Financial Institution, prepares the CIB report of the concerned person in good faith to discharge its statutory obligation which is operated in an automatic software and in the present case, the respondents followed the same procedure and as such, there is no illegality in that respect on the part of the respondents and considering the aforesaid provisions of law and procedure, the learned trial Judge rightly rejected the application for temporary injunction which is ought to be sustained and hence the Rule dated 19-11-2024 is liable to be discharged for not being maintainable. 

8. He next submits that Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 clearly states that "No suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the Bank or any of its officers for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of Article 36 or Article 37 or Article 38 or Article 39 of Article 40 or in pursuance of the provisions of Chapter IV.", and this provision means that the provision under Article 41 has even debarred the entertainment of any suit in respect of such publication by Bangladesh Bank in the CIB report 73 DLR 554 and as such, the learned trial Judge rightly rejected the application of the plaintiff-appellant under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 inasmuch as the suit itself is ought to have been rejected by the trial Court pursuant to Article 41 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972, let alone any temporary injunction and therefore, the appeal and rule issued by the Hon'ble Court on 19-11-2024 are liable to be dismissed and discharged for not being maintainable. 

9. He then submits that it is succinctly clear that the plaintiff-appellant is a default borrower, thereby there is no scope to allow any application as to temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rules I and 2 of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the learned trial judge rightly rejected the same which is liable to be sustained. 

10. He candidly submits that it has also been held in the case of Shirajul Islam Mollah vs Bangladesh Bank reported in 73 DLR 554 that "...Such publication by Bangladesh Bank is immune from any legal challenge through any suit or proceedings under Article 41 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972" and since the suit is barred by law, order of injunction is not tenable in law. 

11. He strenuously submits that from the legal decisions taken in the cases of Shahzada Muhd. limed Beg vs Sultan Mahmood Khan reported in 22 DLR (SC) 41, Hossain Ahmed vs HD Hossain and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 223, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangshta vs Aziz Uddin Chowdhury reported in 7 BLT (AD) (1999) 81 : 51 DLR (AD) 96 and Solar En Foundation and others vs Infrastructure Development Company Limited (IDCOL) and others decided by the larger bench in Civil Rule No. 761 (FM) of 2022 (arising out of FMAT No. 412 of 2022), it is now settled that no injunction can be granted to restrain the defendants from performing the statutory duties and under such circumstances, the appeal and Rule are not maintainable in the eye of law. 

12. He lastly submits that it has been held in the case of Nur Muhammad and others vs Moulvi Mainuddin Ahmed and others, reported in 39 DLR (AD) 1 that—"Where a suit is at its very inception not in law maintainable, the contention that the suit is not maintainable because of mala fide does not arise"; since the suit is barred by law, order of injunction is not tenable in law. 

13. Mr. Mahmud Hasan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 has adopted the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 3. 

14. We have gone through the memorandum of the first miscellaneous appeal, the application for injunction and the materials annexed therewith and perused the same. We have also heard the learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 3 and the learned Deputy Attorney-General along with learned Assistant Attorney-Generals for the Respondent Nos.1 and 2 at length and considered their submissions to the best of our wit and wisdom. 

15. It appears from the record that the plaintiff-appellant is the default borrower as per provision of section 5GaGa of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 and the applicant bank has rightly reported to the Bangladesh Bank for publishing the name of the petitioners in CIB database of Bangladesh Bank and there is no illegality in publishing the name of the petitioner in CIB database by the Bangladesh Bank. 

16. Apart from the above, according to section 45 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991, the Bangladesh Bank is entrusted with the obligation to take the necessary steps in the following matters if satisfied:—
a) in the public interest, or 
b) to provide for the improvement of the monetary policy or banking policy, or 
c) to prevent the affairs of any banking company being conducted in a manner detrimental to the interests of the depositors or in a manner prejudicial to the interest of the banking company; or 
d) to secure the proper management of any banking company.

17. It is stated that as per Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order 1972:—
"No suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the Bank or any of its officers for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of Article 36 or Article 37 or Article 38 or Article 39 or Article 40 or in pursuance of the provisions of chapter IV." 

18. Therefore, as per the above provision, the plaintiff-appellant has no right to file any suit or legal proceeding against the Bank challenging the CIB report published by the Bangladesh Bank. 

19. Furthermore, since the plaintiff-appellant is a default borrower as per provision of section 5GaGa of the Bank Companies Act, 1991, the applicant bank has rightly reported to the Bangladesh Bank for publishing the name of the plaintiff in CIB database of Bangladesh Bank under section 27AA of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 and as such, there is no illegality in sending the plaintiff's report to the Bangladesh Bank by the applicant bank and publication in the CIB database by the Bangladesh Bank. 

20. In addition to the above, from the legal decisions taken in the cases of Shahzada Muhd. timed Beg vs Sultan Mahmood Khan reported in 22 DLR (SC) 41, Hossain Ahmed vs HD Hossain and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 223, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangshta vs Aziz Uddin Chowdhury reported in 7 BLT (AD) ( 1999) 81 and SolarEn Foundation and others vs Infrastructure Development Company Limited (1DCOL) and others decided by the larger bench in Civil Rule No. 761 (FM) of 2022 (arising out of FMAT No. 412 of 2022), it is now settled that no injunction can be granted to restrain the defendants from performing the statutory duties. 

21. It is pertinent to note that in a case where granting of an order of injunction is not permitted by law and where the plaintiff has no prima-facie case, the issue of balance of convenience and inconvenience and the issue of irreparable loss have become immaterial and the balance of convenience and inconvenience lies in rejecting the prayer for injunction, least to save the national economy by saving the banking sector from being collapsed and closed to the great detriment of the depositors with whose fund the banks run their business and to prevent liquidity crisis. 

22. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the propositions of law cited and discussed above, we do not find any substance in the first miscellaneous appeal and the civil Rule. 

23. Consequently, the first miscellaneous appeal is dismissed. 

24. Similarly, for the reasons stated above, the connected civil Rule is also discharged. 

25. The order of injunction granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is recalled and vacated. 

Communicate the judgment and order to the learned judge of the concerned trial court, at once. 

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Abdullah Al Mubin, Advocate … For the Petitioners
Mr. Baki Md. Murtoza, Advocate … For the Opposite Party No. 1
parties:
Md. Faysal Madbar and others ...... Petitioners
Vs.
A Khaleque Sarder and others ..... Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
In this revision Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 28.09.2016 passed by the learned Senior District Judge, Shariatpur, in Title Appeal No. 70 of 2014 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 30.04.2014 (decree signed on 04.05.2014) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Damudya, Shariatpur, in Title Suit No. 10 of 2012 dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the petitioners, as plaintiff, filed Title Suit No. 10 of 2012 against the opposite parties praying for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land claiming that Akkel Ali Sarder and Others were the owners and possessors of land measuring 10.77 Acres within Police Station-Damudya, District Shariatpur under R.S. Khatian No. 327. In that khatian Akkel Ali Sarder has been described and mentioned in 'Cha' group as owner and possessor in R.S. Plot Nos. 4213, 4234, 4630, 4640, 4801, 4802, 4860 and he was shown as sole possessor of 16 decimals land of RS Plot No. 4883. Akkel Ali Sarder transferred the land measuring 90 decimals including the land measuring 16 decimals under R.S Plot. No. 4883 vide Deed of Sale No. 2350 dated 24.08.1950 to Makdam Ali Madbar. Land measuring 16 decimals under R.S. Plot No. 4883 is the suit land. Land purchased by Makdam Ali Madbar stood recorded in his name in S.A. Khatian No. 364 covering Plot Nos. 4213, 4234, 4640, 4880 and 4883 along with others, but in the remark column against S.A. Plot No. 4883 the name of Kalu Sarder has been wrongly mentioned as possessor.

3. Makdam Ali Madbar died leaving behind one son namely (i) Ramiz Uddin Madbar and 3 (three) daughters namely (ii) Jahura Bibi, (iii) Chutu Bibi alias Chotni Bibi and (iv) Paglee Bibi alias Amirjaan Bibi as his successors who acquired the land by inheritance and had been in possession. Thereafter Chutu Bibi sold her portion of land measuring 18 decimals vide Deed of Sale No.7181 dated 29.11.1974 to her brother, Ramiz Uddin Madbar. Afterwards, Ramiz Uddin Madbar died leaving behind 4 sons and 4 daughters named (i) Sirajul Haque Madbar, (ii) Shamsul Haque Madbar, (iii) A. Rahman Madbar, (iv) Daulatunnessa, (v) Amena Begum, (vi) Hamida Begum, (vii) Parvin Begum, (viii) Nasima Begum and (ix) Jaynab Bibi wife of late Ramiz Uddin Madbar. On the other hand another successor of late Makdam Ali Madbar namely Amirjaan Bibi died leaving behind only son named Kalu Hawlader as her legal heir. Subsequently, Kalu Hawlader died leaving behind his only son namely Makbul Hossain Hawlader. Another daughter of late Makdam Ali Madbar named Jahura Khatun being the lawful owner of the suit land along with the aforementioned owners has been in peaceful possession of the suit land for years without any hindrance from any corner.

4. Since the Petitioner's property situated beside a local hat, the Opposite Parties on 19th Paush, 1411 B.S. corresponding to 2nd January, 2005 for their need sought permission from the Petitioner No.1 to build a temporary structure of a shop on a small portion of the suit land. Being requested by the Opposite Parties, the Petitioner No.1 in presence of the witnesses namely (i) A. Hamid Hawlader, (ii) A. Rashid Bepari, (iii) Salamat Kha verbally permitted the Opposite Parties to build a temporary structure of a shop at the west corner of their property on the condition that the Opposite Parties would vacate their possession as and when asked by the Petitioners. Accordingly, the Opposite Party Nos. 1 to 3 built a temporary structure of a shop on the western side of the suit land. On the middle of Sraban month of 1418 B.S., the Petitioners asked the Opposite Parties to vacate the suit land. But the Opposite Parties denied to vacate the same claiming that the Petitioners are not the owners of the suit land as the S.A. khatian stood recorded in the name of their predecessor Kalu Sarder and others, hence, the present suit for declaration and recovery of possession.

5. The defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia that Umed Ali Sarder, Sabulla Sarder, Sayed Ali Sarder. Mantazuddin Sarder, Kalai Sarder and Nawab Ali were the C.S. recorded tenants of land measuring 10.81 Acres covered by various C.S. Plots, under C.S. Khatian No.7. Kalai Sarder died leaving his 2(two) brothers namely (i) Mantazuddin Sarder and (ii) Nawab Ali Sarder as his legal heirs. Then Mantazuddin died leaving behind 3 (three) sons namely (i) Kalu Sarder, (ii) Akkel Ali Sarder and (iii) Kuti Sarder alias Samed Ali Sarder as his legal heirs. While the aforementioned Kalu Sarder and others were in possession of the land their names were duly recorded against various Plot numbers under R.S. Khatian No.327. In 'Cha' group the names of Akkel Ali, Kalu Sarder and Kuti alias Samed Ali Sarder were duly recorded. The entire land measuring 16 decimals under C.S. Plot No. 3308 was wrongly recorded in the name of Akkel Ali instead of recording the names of 03 (three) brothers, Akkel Ali, Kalu Sarder and Kuti alias Samed Ali Sarder. Although land measuring 16 decimals had been recorded in the name of Akkel Ali his brothers namely Kalu Sarder and Kuti alias Samed Ali Sarder were in possession of their respective shares. Accordingly, subsequent S.A. Khatian No. 364 correctly recorded in the names of Kalu Sarder and Others. Kalu Sarder's share in the suit land was 5.75 Decimals. Said Kalu Sarder died leaving behind his sons and daughters namely (i) A Khaleque Sarder, (ii) Hakim Ali Sarder, (iii) Fuljaan Bibi and (iv) Mayful Jaan Bibi.

6. Thus the Opposite Party No.2 acquired land measuring .133 decimal by way of inheritance and he purchased land measuring 3.00 decimals vide Deed of Sale No.824 dated 28.06.1990 from another son of late Mantazuddin Sarder named Kuti Sarder alias Samed Ali Sarder. In this way the Opposite Party No.2 acquired total 4.33 decimals land by way of inheritance and purchase. The Opposite Party No. 2 constructed a shop on the land measuring 1 decimal and has been possessing the entire land by planting trees in the rest of the areas. Akkel Ali had no legal right to transfer entire land measuring 16 decimals under S.A. Plot No. 4883. Akkel Ali was only entitled to get 5.75 decimals, as the land is a joint property, hence the suit was liable to be dismissed and the only remedy for the Petitioners to file a partition suit, as such, the suit is not maintainable in law.

7. The trial court on the basis of pleadings of both the parties framed 5 (five) issues for determination of the matter in dispute between the parties. In course of hearing the plaintiff examined 3 (three) witnesses as P.Ws. and the defendant examined 2 (two) witnesses as D.Ws. Both the parties submitted documents in support of their respective claim which were duly marked as exhibits. The trial court after hearing by its judgment and decree dated 30.04.2014 dismissed the suit.

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial court, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 70 of 2014 before the District Judge, Shariatpur who heard the appeal and after hearing by the impugned judgment and decree dated 28.09.2016 dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial court. At this juncture, the petitioners moved this Court by filing this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

9. Mr. Abdullah Al Mubin, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that in dismissing the suit and appeal both the courts below wrongly held that the suit property is ejmali property of Akkel Ali Sarder, Kalu Sarder, Samed Ali Sarder and their sisters. Since the property has not been partitioned by metes and bound among the cosharers, present suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession against a co-sharer by inheritance is not maintainable in law. He submits that both the courts below failed to consider Sub-Division of R.S. Khatian No. 327 by which the property have been legally partitioned among the co-sharers describing all the tenants by a specific group coupled with their possession and enjoyment. It is also argued that after purchase of the property by Makdam Ali from Akkel Ali Sarder, none of the co-sharers like Kalu Sarder, Samed Ali Sarder or any other heirs of Montazuddin raised any objection regarding title of Akkel Ali and long possession of Makdam Ali in the purchased property. He submits that Akkel Ali Sarder transferred total 90 sataks of land covered by 6 plots in their entirety. The suit Plot No. 4883 contain only 16 sataks which exclusively stood recorded in the name of Akkel Ali Sarder in R.S. Khatian No. 327. Referring R.S. Khatian No. 327 (exhibits- ‘1’ and ‘Ka-1’), he argued that by R.S. record all the property measuring 10.77 acres was partitioned among the recorded owners describing all the groups as ‘Ka’, ‘Kha’, ‘Ga’, ‘Uma’, ‘Cha’, ‘Chha’ and ‘Ja’. Vendor of Makdam Ali belonged to group-‘Cha’ and in his group other heirs of Montazuddin Sarder has not been included, meaning thereby, Akkel Ali Sarder exclusively got his share from the plot against which his name has been exclusively written and mentioned. Said Akkel Ali along with other non-suited plots sold Plot No. 4883 measuring 16 sataks to Makdam Ali as per record of right (exhibit-1).

10. He argued that S.A. khatian has no evidentiary value as decided by this Court in various pronouncement, however, S.A. khatian stood recorded in the name of Makdam Ali and others, but wrongly mentioned that the suit plot is in possession of Kalu and in exhibit-Ka-2 mentioned as Kalu gong. R.S. record has strong evidentiary value, wherein Kalu and others have no right, title and possession in the suit plot. It is submitted that to prove the case of the plaintiffs, they examined 03 (three) witnesses out of which P.W. 2 is Salamat Kha son of Moyfuljan Bibi daughter of Kalu Sarder who in his examination in chief stated that defendant is a permissive possessor under the plaintiffs and at the time of giving permission to raise a temporary shop he was present and also stated that the defendant Abdul Khalek is his maternal uncle. In cross, the defendant could not shake the evidence of P.W. 1 and 2 which can help the defendant. P.W. 3 Abdul Hamed Howlader also stated that at the request of the P.Ws. 2 and 3, the plaintiff No. 1 agreed to accord permission to the defendant to raise a shop on the suit plot, on the condition that he will surrender vacant possession as and when asked by the plaintiff.

11. He submits that Makdam Ali purchased the property in the year 1950, no co-sharer of Akkel Ali during their life time raised any objection. Since purchase Makdam Ali, then his sons and daughters and then the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land and the plaintiffs also purchased some property by sale deed No. 7181 dated 29.11.1974. The plaintiff’s father Ramizuddin has purchased the land from Chuto Bibi @ Chotni Bibi. Both the trial court and the appellate court misread the evidence led by the plaintiffs and the defendants and failed to find that nowhere in the oral evidence, the corroborative witnesses uttered a single word that the suit property is ejmali property, as such, both the courts below committed illegality and error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

12. Mr. Baki Md. Murtoza, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that as per C.S. Khatian No. 7 (exhibit-‘Ka’) property measuring 10 acres 81 sataks belonged to Montazuddin Sarder and others as mentioned in the khatian. Montazuddin was owner of 2 annas 13 gondas 1 kora 1 kranti in the khatian and died leaving 3 (three) sons Akkel Ali Sarder, Kalu Sarder, Samed Ali Sarder, daughter Chutu Bibi, wife Rezia Khatun and another daughter Julekha Bibi, they by inheritance got the property, accordingly, R.S. Khatian No. 327 (exhibit- ‘Ka-1’) stood recorded in their names mentioning their respective share.

13. He submits that though against some plots exclusive possession of Akkel Ali has been mentioned there was no partition among the heirs of Montazuddin and they used to possess the suit property along with other non-suited property left by Montazuddin in ejmali. Akkel Ali one of the son of Montazuddin transferred the suit Plot No. 4883 along with 5 other plots to the predecessor of the plaintiffs in the year 1950, but Akkel Ali had no right, title to transfer entire suit plot measuring 16 sataks which also belonged to Kalu Sarder, Samed Ali Sarder and Chutu Bibi.

14. He submits that Kalu Sarder died leaving Abdul Khalek Sarder, Hakim Ali Sarder, Fuljan Bibi. Defendant No. 2 got .133 decimals of land from Plot No. 4883 by inheritance and he purchased 3 decimals of land by deed No. 824 dated 28.06.1990 from one son of Montazuddin Sarder named Kuti Sarder and Jalal Sarder, Nurul Islam Sarder, both sons of Kalu Sarder. Thus he acquired 4.33 decimals of land by inheritance and purchase. He has been possessing the land by raising shop house on one decimal land and planting various types of trees in the rest land. Akkel Ali Sarder was entitled to get 5.75 decimals, but by the deed of the year 1950, he transferred 16 sataks land of Plot No. 4883. As such, the trial court and the appellate court rightly held and observed that the plaintiffs ought to have filed a suit for partition seeking saham of their purchased land making all the recorded owners as defendants in the suit.

15. It is argued that the plaintiffs utterly failed to prove that the defendant No. 2 got possession of the suit property as permissive possessor under the plaintiff No. 1 rather the defendant could able to prove that he has been possessing the part of suit plot as heir of Kalu Sarder and rest 3 decimal of land by purchase in the year 1990. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendant was inducted in the suit plot and constructed shop house with permission of the plaintiff in the year 2005, whereas, the defendant No. 2 purchased part of the property in the year 1990 before 15 years of alleged permission, as such, in both counts i.e. title of the plaintiffs as well as possession of the plaintiff in the suit property failed, consequently, both the courts below dismissed the suit and appeal observing that without filing a suit for partition the suit is not maintainable in its present form. Moreover, the plaintiff as P.W. 1 in cross unequivocally admitted that there was no legal partition among the heirs of Montazuddin Sarder. In the absence of any legal partition, the present suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession against an admitted co-sharer is not maintainable.

16. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, have gone through the revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, plaint in suit, written statement, evidence both oral and documentary and the impugned judgment and decree of both the courts below.

17. As per C.S. Khatian No. 7 (exhibit-‘Ka’) the suit plot along with many other plots stood recorded in the name of predecessor of the defendant No. 2 Montazuddin Sarder and others as per their share mentioned in the khatian. Montazuddin Sarder died leaving 3 sons, Akkel Ali Sarder, Kalu Sarder, Samed Ali Sarder, daughter Chutu Bibi, wife Rezia Khatun and another Julekha Bibi wife of Hossen Ali Sarder. R.S. Khatian No. 327 stood recorded in the name of heirs of Montazuddin Sarder mentioning their respective share against their names, status of all the tenants are permanent raiyat. The name of tenants in R.S. Khatian No. 327 have been recorded specifying their share in different group like ‘Ka’, ‘Kha’, ‘Ga’, ‘Uma’, ‘Cha’, ‘Chha’ and ‘Ja’ which is not denied by both the parties. Had it been so, R.S. khatian shows that Akkel Ali Sarder is owner of 8 gondas, 1 kora, 2 kranti, 16 danto and his name stood recorded independently in ‘Cha’ group having no other co-sharers with him like groups ‘Ka’, ‘Kha’, ‘Ga’, ‘Uma’, ‘Chha’ and ‘Ja’. All the tenants name as a recorded in R.S. khatian has been specifically mentioned against each plot mentioning who owns the plot as owner and possessor. Because of mentioning the name of tenant against each plot it can be easily presumed and construed that respective plot as mentioned in the khatian was in possession of that person by amicable partition or arrangement among the co-sharers. As per R.S. record Akkel Ali Sarder exclusively got some plots in his share and only Plot No. 4480 having 8 annas share with his brother Kalu Sarder and others measuring 10 sataks. He transferred the property measuring 90 sataks including suit plot measuring 16 sataks to Makdam Ali Sarder by a registered deed No. 2350 dated 24.08.1950, original of which has been filed by the plaintiff as exhibit-‘2Ka’. As per claim of the plaintiff Makdam Ali after purchase got possession from Akkel Ali Sarder and had been possessing the same with the knowledge of other brothers of Akkel Ali Sarder, but none of them raised any objection against the sale by Akkel Ali Sarder and possession of Makdam Ali Matbar.

18. In S.A. khatian name of Makdam Ali Matbar has been correctly recorded, but share of the tenants has not been mentioned as the khatian was prepared without any field survey. The plaintiffs claimed that Makdam Ali, then his sons were in possession of the suit plot, but said wrong was not in the knowledge of the plaintiffs. The suit property is located beside a local hat. The defendant No. 2 on 19th Poush 1411 B.S. corresponding to 02.01.2005 along with P.W. 2 Salamat Kha and P.W. 3 Abdul Hamed Hawlader requested the plaintiff to allow defendant No. 2 to build a temporary structure of a shop on the suit land. The plaintiff at the request of witnesses permitted the defendant No. 2 to build a temporary structure of a shop on the suit plot measuring 12 feet ^ 8 feet, on the condition that he will vacate possession as and when asked by the plaintiff, accordingly, the defendant No. 2 raised a shop house on the south-western side of the suit land and used to possess the same as permissive possessor.

19. At the middle of Srabon 1418 B.S. the plaintiffs asked the defendant to vacate the possession of suit land, but he denied claiming that the plaintiffs are not the owners of the suit land and disclosed that in S.A. khatian their predecessors name appearing. The defendant No. 2 claimed that he as heir of Kalu Sarder inherited .133 decimals of land and he purchased 3 decimals of land from Kuti Sarder son of Montazuddin and his brothers by a registered deed No. 824 dated 28.06.1990, thus he acquired 4.33 decimals of land by inheritance and by purchase. He claimed that he never took permission from the plaintiffs to build a shop house on the western corner of the suit plot. Rather he has been possessing the suit property right from R.S. record through his predecessor Kalu Sarder and his uncle and then presently the defendant No. 2 himself. The story of taking permissive possession from plaintiff No.1 is false and fabricated. It is also claimed that the plaintiff filed Miscellaneous Petition Case No. 372 of 2010 against the defendant before the ADM, Shariatpur under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, wherein, the property was physically enquired by Union Land Assistant Officer, Puneshor Union Land Office, Damudya who furnished report finding that the defendant No. 2 is in possession of a shop measuring 1 satak and in that report it has been stated that the defendant is in possession of the suit property since 10-15 years which clearly proves that the defendant No. 2 was in possession of the suit property by dint of inheritance and by purchase not by taking permission from the plaintiffs as alleged. After receipt of report learned ADM, Shariatpur by order dated 21.12.2011 filed the case directing defendant No. 2 not to enter into the property under possession of the plaintiffs. Therefore, the plaintiff has no cause of action for filing the suit as the evidences established that the defendant No. 2 possessing the suit land by inheritance and purchase not with the permission of the plaintiff as permissive possessor.

20. The trial court while dismissing the suit put importance on the evidence of plaintiff who stated that the property left by Montazuddin Sarder inherited by his heirs, among them no legal partition has been done, as such, the defendant being a co-sharer by inheritance in the property cannot be evicted without bringing a suit for partition making all the recorded tenants as defendants in suit. The appellate court also concurred the observation made by the trial court in toto and dismissed the appeal only on the point of maintainability of the suit without a suit for partition.

21. Now the question before us, whether R.S. recorded tenant Akkel Ali Sarder owned the property transferred to Makdam Ali exclusively without legal partition among all the heirs of Montazuddin Sarder. Parties to the proceeding unequivocally admitted that Akkel Ali one of the sons of Montazuddin who sold the same to Makdam Ali Sarder. The question raised by the defendant is that since the suit plot is ejmali property of all the heirs of Montazuddin Sarder, Akkel Ali Sarder had no right or title to transfer entire 16 sataks of land under Plot No. 4883 to Makdam Ali, but other plots also transferred by Akkel Ali in their entirety which has not been challenged by the predecessor of the defendants named Kalu Sarder, Samed Ali or any other brother and sisters. It is also not the case of defendant that though Makdam Ali purchased the property from Akkel Ali in the year 1950, Makdam Ali Sarder never delivered with possession of the property purchased by him. Except the suit plot, the defendants kept them silent about other property transferred by Akkel Ali Sarder.

22. To appreciate the fact, whether Akkel Ali had title and possession in the plots under R.S. Khatian No. 327 mentioned against his name and transferred to Makdam Ali. R.S. Khatian No. 327 (exhibit-‘1’) and (exhibit-‘Ka-1’) shows that in ‘Ka’ group Omed Ali Sarder, in ‘Kha’ group Hatem Ali and others, in ‘Ga’ group Kabil Sarder and others in ‘Uma’ group Kalu Sarder and other heirs of Montazuddin and in ‘Cha’ group only Akkel Ali Sarder, in ‘Chha’ group Nawab Ali Sarder and ‘Ja’ group Khadem Ali Sarder. As per their group, possession has been mentioned against the plot who is owner and possessor of the property. Suit Plot No. 4883 measuring 16 sataks along with other plots have been specifically mentioned under exclusive possession of Akkel Ali Sarder. Having no other co-sharer in this particular suit plot like Plot No. 4480 mentioning separate group connotes that the property covered by all the plots have been amicably partitioned among the tenants giving different group and mentioning their names against each plot. Though the property has not been partitioned by any deed of partition or a partition decree of the court but the record of right itself partitioned the property separating all the tenants from each other. Since Akkel Ali as per record in ‘Cha’ group mentioning his name against some plots, his other brothers or sisters are not co-sharer in that plot, that is why, after transfer of the property by Akkel Ali Sarder in favour of Makdam Ali his brothers, sisters or mother raised no objection against the said transfer. After purchase Makdam Ali was in possession of the purchased land, accordingly, S.A. Khatian No. 364 stood recorded in his name along with other co-sharers without mentioning their respective share, it does not mean that because of not mentioning his name against plot in S.A. khatian, transfer made by Akkel Ali Sarder lost its validity.

23. Evidence led by defendant No. 2 himself and D.W. 2 coupled with report furnished by the inquiry officer in Miscellaneous Petition No. 372 of 2010, the defendant No. 2 is in possession of 1 satak land only which is claimed by the plaintiff. The defendant No. 2 though claimed that he purchased 3 sataks of land from sons of Kalu Sarder and others in the year 1990, but could not establish his possession in purchased property by any evidence except a deed of sale of the year 1990. Had the defendant No. 2 purchased the property in the year 1990 and got delivery of possession at that time. He would not have built a shop measuring 12 feet ^ 8 feet at the western corner of the suit plot. Except the defendant No. 2 none of the heirs of Kalu Sarder or other heirs claimed the property from the plaintiff. P.W. 2 is nephew of defendant No. 2 who on oath stated that at the request of P.Ws. 2 and 3 the plaintiff gave permission to the defendant No. 2 to build a temporary shop at the west corner of the suit plot. By cross examination nothing could bring adverse to the evidence led by P.Ws. 1-3 to establish that the defendant No. 2 entered into possession or have been possessing the suit plot by inheritance or by purchase from one of the heirs of Samed Ali.

24. Moreover, S.A. khatian stood recorded independently for specific portion of the property in the name of Akkel Ali, Makdam Ali and predecessor of defendant No. 2 Kalu Sarder and others as son of Omed Ali. The defendant could not explain or raise any objection that Kalu Sarder, Samed Ali are not sons of Omed Ali, but they are sons of Montazuddin Sarder. Both the parties to the proceeding kept them mum about this anomalies in the khatian. If I consider that Kalu Sarder, Samed Ali are sons of Omed Ali the case of the defendant as made out in the defense has no basis as they are claiming the property through Montazuddin Sarder whose name is totally absent in S.A. khatian. Now it is settled principle of law that if a person entered into any property as tenant or as permissive possessor or with the consent of the owner of the property claims title in the property is to surrender possession to the plaintiff first. In the present case had the defendant No. 2 acquired title in the property by inheritance and by purchase he is to surrender the possession to the plaintiff first and then he can come with his claim of title by filing properly constituted suit as the defendant No. 2 failed to establish that he is in possession of the property through his predecessor Kalu Sarder or by purchase from heirs of Samed Ali. In claiming so the defendant No. 2 is to prove first that Kalu Sarder was one of the owner of the property as per record of right and to prove that Akkel Ali was not owner of the entire plot and there was no partition.

25. Unless the R.S. record of right stands now is corrected or otherwise proved incorrect, I find that Akkel Ali being exclusive owner in possession of plot No. 4883 had every right to transfer the same to Makdam Ali. Apart from this a co-sharer of a joint property if transfers any property from any particular plot and delivered possession not exceeding his share is a valid transfer and in that case the claimant who challenged the transfers is to come with a suit for partition. Both the courts below failed to appreciate the oral evidence, documentary evidence as well as evidence led by defendant No. 2 and superficially observed that unless a suit for partition is filed by the plaintiff, present suit is not maintainable. As such, both the courts below in dismissing the suit and disallowing the appeal committed illegality and error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice, as they have failed to appreciate the status of the tenants in different groups as recorded in R.S. Khatian No. 327.

26. It is to be noted here that in Mufassil District when the learned Advocates drafting plaint or written statement usually mentioned the date month and Bengali year without mentioning corresponding date, month and English year which sometime create confusion in deciding the the dispute between the parties. Moreover, almost in every cases the Mufassil’s learned Advocates mentioned the plaintiff as “সাহেল” “মজহর” and the defendant as “তরফসানি” (Tarafsani). Nowadays all those terms creates confusion in identifying the parties. Because of modernization and for easy understanding it is advised not to use such terms in drafting plaint and petition in miscellaneous cases describing the petitioner, opposite party, plaintiff and defendant with the aforesaid words “সাহেল”, “মজহর”, “তরফসানি” (Tarafsani). Because of this situation, I am inclined to direct the Registrar General to issue a circular for all the Mufassil District Bar Association and the concern District Judge informing them to comply with the order of this Court describing the petitioner and opposite parties in all miscellaneous cases and plaintiff and defendant in original suits or original proceeding as “Petitioner”, “Opposite Party”, “Plaintiff” “Defendant” respectively to avoid confusion regarding identity of the parties to the suit and to mention date month and year in the plaint and written statement as per English Calendar.

27. Taking into consideration the above, I find merit in the rule as well as in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.

28. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs.

29. Judgment and decree of both the courts below are hereby set aside. The suit is decreed against the defendant No. 2 on contest and ex parte against the rest. The defendant No. 2 is hereby directed to hand over vacant possession of the suit land to the plaintiffs within 30 days from date failing which the plaintiffs shall be entitled to get possession of the suit land through court.

Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concerned and send down the lower court records at once.

End.

Mr. Md. Sujad Miah, Advocate ------- For the Respondent No. 1.
Mr. Md. Mohsin Kabir, D.A.G with Mr. A.K.M. Rezaul Karim Khandaker, D.A.G with Ms. Shahin Sultana, A.A.G with Mr. Md. Manowarul Islam Uzzal, A.A.G with Mr. Md. Moklesur Rahman, A.A.G ------- For the Government.
