The learned,Additional District Judge passed the order dated 3-4-69 holding that the very same matter was raised by the plaintiff firm in its application dated 11-5-68 which was in substance an application nuclei section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure although it purported to be one under sections 152 and 153 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the plaintiff firm not entitle to reagitate the same matter under section 47 of the Code Procedure whist had once before been disposed of by the said Court. On merits also the learned Additional District Judge found the said order to be no inconsistent with equity and justice. The learn and Additional District Judge further belt that, in any view of the matter, when the Court which could pass orders rightly or wrongly had passed the impugned order and the borrower firm did not avail itself of the earliest opportunity to challenge it which they could have done by attacking it before the High Court in F.M.A. III of 1965 as well, the said order could not be declared to be nullity. The borrower firm moved the High Court at Dacca against the said order of the learned Additional District Judge dated 3-4-69 under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure upon which Civil Rule No. 597 of 1969 was issued. At the time of the hearing of the said rule it was held that the impugned order being one under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure was appealable and as such the Civil revision case was not maintainable. The High Court, however, permitted the petition on which the rule was issued to be converted into a Memorandum of Appeal which was then registered as F. M A. No. 81 of 1969. A Division Bench of the High Court (A. S. Chowdhury and N. Islam JJ) took the view in the said case that the application of the Bank dated 21-8-65 was in effect one for review under Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Judges dismissed the appeal by their judgment dated 16-3-69 and gave their decision in the following words:—

"In this case it will appear that the error which was rectified was apparent on the face of the record and that the prayer for reviewing the order was made within 3 weeks from the date of the earlier order. Whether such an order could legally be passed or not, the executing Court cannot sit in judgment over the Trial Court as to whether or not the order of review was legal".

7. The borrower firm filed an application to the Supreme Court of Pakistan for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against the aforesaid judgment of the High Court and the Supreme Court rejected the application by its order dated 9-12-69 on the following view:—

"When execution was started for realization of directly dues an application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed challenging the amendment of the decree as a nullity. Both the Courts below repelled this contention and held that the executing Court cannot go behind the decree."

*******               ******

"The High Court has rightly found that the order of amendment was passed under Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

After the disposal of the above mentioned application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Pakistan the borrower firm has instituted the suit being other Suit No. 69 of 1969 on 26-12-69 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for a declaration that the order of amendment passed on 21-8-65 was illegal, fraudulent, without jurisdiction and void and that the defendant was not entitled to proceed with the execution of the said order. The grounds on the basis of which the said order was impugned have been enumerated in paragraph 14 of the plaint in the following manner:

Grounds:

"(a) That under the law where the original decree is with respect to interest the Court must be deemed to have refused it there is no inherent power in the Court toward interest in such a case. The Court has contravened the principles of law the order passed is without jurisdiction and void.

(b) That the interest not awarded by the original device cannot be awarded by way of amendment of the decrees and as such the order is nullity.

(c) That the statute constituting the defdts does not make any provision for the purpose.

As the Defdt. has acted beyond the provision of the Act, his action in the matter of getting peal interest and costs is illegal and without jurisdiction.

(d) That as the said order of amendment has been procured without the regular personal service of notice on the order is illegal, fraudulent without jurisdiction. As there is a change of front by the so called amendment the notice ought to have been served upon the plaintiff personally. The service of notice on the lawyer in view of the fact of creating change of front is no service on the plffs. and as such this makes the entire order of amendment without jurisdiction and void.

(e) That in view of the fact and law that the order was without jurisdiction and void the executing Court was powerful enough to go behind the decree. Non-interference by the executing Court in this respect makes the order of the executing Court also illegal and void without jurisdiction.

(f) That the defdt. misled the Court by all means without allowing the Court to know that the defdt. by such procedure for amendment was going to change the front. As the learned Court was misled thereby the order is frequent and without jurisdiction.

(g) That the defdt. by the aforesaid contrivance kept the Court and the plaintiff in ignorance of the real truth and law and thereby the managed to procure, the illegal and fraudulent order."

8. Having regard to the contentions raised in this Court on behalf of the borrower concerned that the District Judge acting under section 39 of the Ordinance is not a Court, advocate has therefore argued that the said Court but a persona designata and that as such the Additional District Judge had no jurisdiction to hear the  proceeding under section 39 of the Ordinance, it may be pointed out here that the validity of the order passed on 24-7-65 has not then assailed nor the competence of the Judge who passed either of the orders has been questioned. On the contrary, the order passed on the 24th July, 1965 by the learned Additional District Judge has been freely described as a decree and the learned Judge has been referred to as the Court.

9. Immediately after the institution of the said suit an application was filed on behalf of the plaintiff on the 27th of December 1969 for temporary injunction purporting to restrain the opposite party from executing the decree passed in the Miscellaneous Case No.51 of 1969 in the Court of the Additional District Judge, Chittagong. Upon the said application notice was directed to be issued upon the defendant Bank with an order of the said application. The defendant Bank thereafter appeared in the suit and filed an application of objection opposing the prayer of the plaintiff for temporary injunction. The learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 26-9-70 rejected the prayer for temporary injunction on the view that the plaintiff had failed to make out a prima facie case but directed that the mortgaged and hypothecated properties should be sold for realization of Rs. 3,66,491,51 paisa only and the excess sale proceeds should remain in deposit in Court  pending disposal of the suit. Both the plaintiff and the defendant Bank have filed appeals against the said order.

10. Mr. Moinul Huq appearing on behalf of the plaintiff appellant in F. M. A 29 of 1971, has contended that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in holding that the plaintiff had failed to make out a prima facie case. In

developing his contention the learned advocate has raised a point which was not taken at any stage of the suit. He contends that the impugned order of amendment passed by the learned Additional District Judge  had no jurisdiction to try and dispose of a proceeding under section 39 of the Ordinance.

11. In order to substantiate his contentions, Mr. Moinul Huq submits that the District Judge acting under the provision of section 39 of the Ordinance was a mere persona designate and therefore had no power to transfer the proceeding to the Court of the Additional District Judge for a disposal. The learned advocate has therefore argued that the said court of the additional District Judge did not acquire, by virtue of the aforesaid transfer, any jurisdiction to dispose of the proceedings under section 39 of the Ordinance.

12. This plea has not found any place in the pleadings of the plaintiff, and is rather contrary to the avertments made therein. For the first time such a plea has been mentioned in the grounds of appeal taken in this court and Mr. Moinul Huq has vigorously put forward this plea for the purpose of showing that the impugned order of amendment was, on the face of it, a nullity, and that as such the plaintiff has been able to make a prima facie case.

The learned advocate for the borrower Firm has also contended that the said order having been passed without serving any notice upon the defdt. Bank was a nullity.

<u>13. Relying upon a decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, namely, Mian Mohammad Latif Vs. Province of West Pakistan, reported in 22 DLR (SC) 98, Mr. Moinul Huq has contended at the outside that the only thing he has to show in his proceedings is that the plaintiff has a good prima facie case meaning thereby that a serious question of law is to be tried in the suit and that in the event of success, if the injunction is not issued the pltf. will suffer an irreparable injury. This is a well established principal of law, which provides a correct guideline for the court which considers the question of making an order of temporary injunction. But the court has to be satisfied that there is really a serious question to be tried in the suit, the answer whereto cannot be immediately found in any statutory or judicial authority. For that reason, we cannot avoid examining</u>

<u>the nature of the questions raised and their seriousness, before it is decided to restrain the actions of the dfdt. which may be otherwise lawful.</u>

14. In order to determine whether the pltf. has been able to make out a prima facie case whether the learned subordinate Judge was right in refusing the order of temporary injunction we shall have to look into the case made out in the court below. Although considerable amount of energy and time was spent by the learned lawyers at the Bar on the vexed question as to whether the "District Judge" under section 39 of the Ordinance is a court or a persona designata, it is not only that such a plea was not taken in pleading or at any stage of the proceeding for injunction but that such a plea is clearly inconsistent with the entire pleading of the pltf. which accepts the validity of the order passed on 24.07.65 by the self-same additional District Judge and describes the said Judge as a Court and his order as a decree of the court.

15. Order 6, role 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which is quoted below is a clear bar against taking such a plea:

No pleading shall, except by way of amendment, raise any new ground of claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the party pleading the same".

The appellants are to succeed on the basis of the case they have made out in the pleadings and urged in the Court below for the purpose of establishing a prima facie case was that the order passed on 21-8-65 amending the decree of the Court having been made without service of any notice upon the appellants was a nullity. The learned Subordinate Judge has repelled this contention on the reasoning that the plaintiff had fought up to the Supreme Court in various ways and that the question in the suit was unsuccessfully raised and canvassed in a Miscellaneous Case which was, in the opinion of the superior Tribunal, a proceeding under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure; and held, in this view of the matter, that the plaintiff has not been able to make out a prima facie case.

16. The learned advocate for the plaintiff, in support of is contention in this regard has relied upon the case of Abdul Hakim Chowdhury Vs Hemchandra Das, reported in 1915 (AIR) Cal. 666 same case 42 Cal. 433, Suruj  Pal Panday and others vs. Utim Pandy and others, reported in 1922 Pat. 281 and Anis Imam and another Vs. Daughter of Jamuna Bai and others, reported in AIR 1949 Pat. 117. These cases do not state anything more than what is provided in provisio (a) to Order 47, rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The said proviso enacts that no application for review shall be granted without previous notices to the opposite party to enable him to appear and be heard in support of the decree or order, a review of which is applied for.

<u>17. Mr  Rafiqul Huq, the learned Advocate for the Bank submits that it is not correct that no notice was served upon the opposite party before granting the application. As a matter of fact, a copy of the notice was served upon the lawyer appearing on behalf of the opposite party and the said lawyer, in fact, appeared at the hearing of the review application and contested the same. The impugned order itself shows that the Court heard both parties. Mr. Moinul Huq has sought to argue that after the passing of the order dated 24-7-65 which was in the nature of a decree, the lawyer for the defendant opposite party became officio and as such had no jurisdiction to accept the aforesaid notice on behalf of his client. That this contention of Mr. Moinul Huq has absolutely no substance will be evident from the provisions of sub-rules (1), (2) and (3) of rule 4, and rule 5 of Order 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure which are to the following effect: —</u>

<u>Order 3. rule 4:</u>

<u>(1) No pleader shall act for any person in any Court, unless he has been appointed for the purpose by such person by a document in writing signed by such person or by his recognized agent or by some other person duly authorized by or under a power of attorney to make such appointment.</u>

<u>(2) Every such appointment shall be filed in Court and shall be deemed to be in force until determined with the leave of the Court by a writing signed by the client or the pleader as the case may be, and filed in Court, or until the client or the pleader dies or until all proceedings in the suit are ended so far as regards the client.</u>

<u>(3) For the purpose of sub-rule (2), an application for review of judgment on application under section 144 or section 152 of this Code, any appeal from any decree or order in the suit and any application or act for the purpose of obtaining copies of documents or return of documents produced or filed in the suit or of obtaining refund of monies paid into the Court in connection with the suit shall be deemed to be proceedings in the suit.</u>

<u>******** ************ **********</u>

<u>Order 3, rule 5:</u>

<u>Any process served on the pleader of any party or left at the office or ordinary residence of such pleader and whether the same is for the personal appearance of the party or not, shall be presumed to be duly communicated and made known to the party whom the pleader represents, and unless the Court otherwise directs shall be as effectual for all purposes as if the same had been given to or served on the party in person".</u>

<u>It is clear from these provisions that the learned lawyer who appeared on behalf of the opposite party at the earlier stage of the proceeding in accordance with the provision of sub-rule (1) of rule 4 of Order 3 of the Code had his authority continuing under sub rule (2) of the said rule until the proceedings itself was brought to a close and in accordance with sub-rule (3) of the said rule an application for review is a proceeding in the suit itself. It is to be noticed in this connection that according to rule 5 any process served on the pleader of any party shall be presumed to be duly communicated and made known to the party whom the pleader represents and it shall be as effectual for all purposes as if the same had been given to or served upon the party in person. Therefore there is no substance in this contention of the learned advocate for the appellant.</u>

<u>There is another aspect of the matter which will show that this objection taken by the learned advocate for appellant is absolutely untenable.</u>

<u>18. The correctness and legality of the order dated 21.05.65 was mooted by the opposite party by means of an application for amendment of the decree filed on 14.05.68 in the original proceeding by reducing rate of interest from 9 1/2 % to 6 1/2 %. This application which was described to be under sections 152 and 153 read with section 151 of the Code was rejected by the learned Judge on the ground that the order awarding interest was passed in presence of the parties and therefore there is no scope for amending or altering it. A rule was issued in Civil Revision No. 704 of 1968 by the HC in respect of the said order, but the revision case was ultimately abandoned. Now this question was the legality of the aforesaid order being passed without any service of notice as contemplated in Order 47, Rule 4(2) proviso (a), could have been and should have been raised in the said proceeding for amendment of the rate of interest, and this having not been done, this question is clearly barred under the principle of constructive res judicata. Furthermore, this very question was subsequently specifically raised after abandoning the revision case in the HC, in an application described to be one under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Filed before the Learned Addtl. District Judge, taking him to be a Court executing the order dated 24.07.65, as amended on 21.08.65 as if it were a decree. The Learned Addtl. District Judge held that the question was res judicata and also that the order complained was not bad. The HC being moved under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure was of the view that   the order passed on 24-07-65 was in the nature of a decree and the application for amendment purporting to be under section 152 and 153 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was, in effect, an application for review under Order 47 of the Code. According to the learned judges of the HC, the learned Additional District Judge while disposing of the said application under section 47 of the Code was an executing court and therefore the said court could not go behind the decree and enquire whether the said order was legally passed. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in an application for leave to appeal affirmed the view of the HC and held that the HC was right in holding that the impugned order of amendment was passed under Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The upshot of this series of the litigation is that according to the Highest judicial authority of the time of the dispute as to the impugned amendment was a matter relating to executability of a portion of the operative order covered by the said amendment and the executing court could not enquire into the legality or validity of of the order under execution. It was therefore the decision of the HC as affirmed by the SC  by necessary implication that the dispute order was not without jurisdiction, because, had it been so the executing court would not have been deterred from holding it to be so. The question as to whether the order of the amendment is without jurisdiction and as a nullity has been decided constructively if not positively in earlier phase of the litigation and as such is prima facie barred by the principle of res judicata.</u>

19. Mr. Moinul Huq has argued, for the purpose of countering the plea of res judicata, that there cannot be a question of res judicata if the former Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit in evidence as conclusive and  in order to find whether the former Court had jurisdiction to try the subsequent suit, it is the jurisdiction of the original Court and not that of the Appellate Court which is to be taken in to consideration. The learned Advocate cited the cases of Secretary of State Vs. Brajendra Kishore, reported in AIR 1936 Cal. 629 Misir Raghobar Dali Vs. Raja Sheo Baksh Singh, reported in LR 9 I.A. 197 and Bharisilal Chowdhury Vs. Sarat Chandra Dass, reported in ILR 23 Cal, 415. These cases lay down the principle on an interpretation of the provision relating to res judicata as embodied in the Code of Civil Procedure, that there will be no res judicata when the former Court had no jurisdiction to try the subsequent suit even though the adverse decision was given by Appellate Court.

<u>20. These decisions have no application to the facts of this case. The main question raised in this suit is whether the order of amendment passed by the learned Additional District Judge dated 21-8-65 was without jurisdiction. An appeal was taken to the High Court against the order dated 24-7-65, but the said appeal the question of validity of the order dated 21-8-65 does not appear to have been raised. But this very question was put into issue, when an application was filed on 14-5-68 before the learned Additional District Judge for amendment of the order dated 21-8-65 by reducing the rate of interest payable on the amount of the debt. This application was rejected on the ground that there was no scope for amendment or modification of the order, as it was passed in presence of the parties. A Civil Rule was issued by the High Court when an application was moved against the said order or rejection but the said Revision Case was ultimately given up. The jurisdiction of the Court of Additional district Judge was invoked by the aforesaid application under sections 152 and 153 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the said Court held that the order passed by the learned Additional District Judge on 21-8-65 could not be varied or altered. It cannot be said that the Court of the Additional District Judge rejecting the said application as a Court of Original jurisdiction was not competent to try the present suit. It may be pointed here that the provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure which requires the institution of a suit in the Court of the lowest grade is a rule of procedure, and not of jurisdiction. In view of the said order of rejection, the question as to the validity of the order dated 21-8-65 appears therefore to be clearly barred by res judicata. Moreover, the same question was again raised before the learned Additional District Judge under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, taking the learned Additional District Judge as an executing Court. The learned Addl. District Judge having held, inter alia, that the question was barred by the principle of res judicata again negative the contention of the Borrower Firm and on appeal the High Court, affirmed the order of the learned Addl. District judge on the view that the impugned order of amendment was passed in exercise of the power of review, and the executing Court could not go behind the decree. By the said order the HC held by necessary implication and constructively that the said order passed in review was not without jurisdiction. On an application for leave to appeal, SC of Pakistan concerned in the aforesaid view of the Dacca HC. Now, that very question has again been raised in this suit, which seems to be doubly barred on account of the general principle of res judicata.</u>

<u>21. We like to refer in this connection. to one case of Indian jurisdiction, viz, Usha Devi vs. Devidas, as reported in AIR 1955 Bom. 239. A compromise decree between the landlord and the tenant was passed in a suit by which the tenant agreed to vacate the premises in suit by a certain date. On the failure of the tenant to vacate, as agreed to, the landlord applied for execution whereupon the executing court ordered possession. An objection was taken on behalf of the tenant on the ground that after the compromise decree a new tenancy was created and the tenancy was protected by the Rent Act. The executing Court having rejected the said objection, the appeals which were successively filed in the Court of the district judge and the HC were dismissed. Thereafter a fresh warrant of possession having been issued by the executing Court, a new objection was taken by the judgment debtor at that stage to the effect that the court which passed the compromise decree had no jurisdiction to try the suit, and as such the compromise decree was a nullity. This new objection being rejected by the executing Court as well as by the District Court, the matter was brought before the HC of Bombay which affirmed the decision of the Courts below on the view that the consideration of the new plea is barred by the general principle of res judicata as is applicable to execution proceedings Chief Justice Chagla in delivering his judgment observe as follows:-</u>

<u>"It is not disputes that if the principle of constructive res judicata were to apply, the petitioner would not be able to challenge the execution proceedings on a ground which she could have put forward earlier and which she failed to do. What is urged by Mr. Desai is that the principle of constructive res judicata does not apply when the question of jurisdiction has been raised. I fail to understand on what principle an exception can be made to the principle of constructive  res judicata when we are dealing with a question of jurisdiction.</u>

<u>******** ************* *****************</u>

<u>Now, it cannot be disputed that if the High Court had held that the Court had jurisdiction, there would have been a finality as far as that decision went and it would not have been open to the petitioner again to raise that contention. It is difficult to understand why a similar finality cannot be given by the fact that the petitioner had failed to raise that contention and the High Court constructively decided that the Court had jurisdiction to execute the decree."</u>

<u>We find ourselves in respectful agreement with this view of the learned Chief Justice.</u>

22. Another contention which Mr Moinul Huq seemed to have argued with all seriousness was that even if the "District Judge" as used in section 39 of the Ordinance meant the Court of District Judge, the Additional District Judge would still be incompetent to entertain the proceeding in question, as there was no valid transfer of the proceeding to his Court. According to the learned Advocate the legislature having made the specific provision that it would be the District Judge who would try a proceeding under section 39 of the Ordinance the District Judge acted beyond jurisdiction in transferring the particular case to the Additional District Judge when it does not appear that there was general assignment of all business by District Judge to the Additional District Judge under section 8(2) of the East Bengal Civil Courts Act. Reliance was placed by him on the cases of Mohamed Musa Vs Abdul Hassan Khan, as reported in ILR, 41 Cal. 866 and Mohabar Rahman Vs. Abdur Rahim, as reported in ILR. 48 Cal. 53. In the first case a Division Bench of Calcutta High Court laid down that an Additional District Judge who was not vested with the power of trying suits under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the Local Government had no jurisdiction to try such suits, and transfer of such a suit under section 24 of the Code by the District Judge to the Additional District Judge was not competent, as there no prior general assignment of the functions of the District Judge to the Additional District Judge. In the second case, it was held that an Additional District Judge by virtue of the assignment of all the functions of a District Judge under the provisions of sub-sec. (2) of section 8 of the Civil Courts Act was empowered to exercise the same powers as the District Judge in suits under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure The latter case does not appear to have much relevance for our present purpose.

23. This contention, which has been raised for the first time in this Court, requires ascertainment of a certain question of fact, namely whether in this particular case there had been a prior assignment of the functions of the District Judge to the Additional District Judge under Civil Courts Act. Though Mr Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate for the borrower concerned has submitted that he has,as requires, ascertained that there was no such prior general assignment of functions, we do not think that we can go into that question at this stage and start an investigation for ascertaining a question of fact, and then determine on the basis of the result of this investigation whether a prima facie case has been established.

<u>24. This contention of Mr. Moinul Huq does, however, otherwise also lack in substance, as it did not take note of the Full Bench Division of Calcutta High Court, viz, Rup-kishore Lal Vs. Neman Bibi, as reported in ILR, 42 Cal. 842 same case 19 CWN. 991, which overruled the case reported in ILR, 41 Cal. 866 and held that it was competent to District Judge to transfer a particular case to an Additional District Judge under sub-sec. (2) of sec. 8 of the Civil Courts Act. 1887. In this case, a proceeding for grant of letters of Administration which under the Probate made Administration Act could have been made by the District Judge, was transferred by the District Judge to an Additional District Judge, although there was no prior general assignment of functions of the District Judge to the Addl. District Judge. We, therefore do not find any substance in the above contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff Firm.</u>

25. The main theme, however, which Mr Moinul Huq has tried to develop in this appeal for the purpose of she wing that the plaintiffs have a prima facie case is that, as we have noticed above, that the District Judge, as used in section 39 of the Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan Ordinance connotes persona designate and not a Court of District Judge The learned Advocate has contended that the Additional District Judge who passed the order dated 21-8-65 had no jurisdiction to pass the said order because, firstly, the term 'district Judge', does not include an Additional District Judge for the purpose of exercising powers under section 39 of the Ordinance and also because the District Judge being not a Court within the meaning of section 8 of the East Bengal Civil Courts Act or under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure had no power to transfer the proceeding in question to the Court of Additional District Judge.

26. We have already indicated that in our view there is no prima facie case in respect of this question as the consideration of this question in the suit, appears to be barred under the rule of pleadings, section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also under the principle of constructive res judicata. But since this question was argued at the bar at considerable length, we have tried to examine this question also in a general way for the purpose of ascertaining if a prima facie case can be said to have been made out on the merits of this question.

<u>27. The Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan Ordinance having not defined the District Judge as including an additional District Judge, prima facie, it can be argued that in view of the provision of section 39 of the Ordinance an Additional District Judge cannot exercise the powers conferred by the said section on a District Judge But if "the District Judge" can be interpreted to mean the Court of District Judge then there will be no difficulty in having the matter heard by an Additional District Judge as the function of a District Judge in respect of a particular case can be transferred by the Court of District Judge to the Court of Additional District Judge.</u>

28. But the question is what is a Court? There may be various kinds of Courts but the Courts with which we are concerned at the present moment are the Courts of law.

29. Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate for the borrower firm has contended that District Judge entertaining a proceeding under section 39 of the Ordinance do not act as a Court but as a persona designate. According to him, the nature of the works which have been assigned to a District Judge under the aforesaid provision of the Ordinance is not a judicial one but is more or less a mechanical one because in certain matters the Judge has no option but to make a particular order and the dominant intent of the legislature is that the District Judge shall function as a part of the Industrial Development Bank for carrying out the Banks business Mr. Rafiqul Huq the learned Advocate for the creditor Bank has, on the other hand, contended that for the purpose of determining the true character of the tribunal, namely, whether it is a Court or a persona designate, we shall have to examine its constitution, the function it discharges and the procedure which it follows: in discharging the said function, and on an examination of these factors in respite of the District Judge acting under the provision of section 39 of the Ordinance it will be clear that it functions as a Court and not as a persona designate Several decisions have been cited at the bar in support of the respective propositions out of which reference may be made to the cases of Afsaruddin Vs. Wazed Ali Khan and another, report in 4 DLR, 442, Most. Dirji Vs, Smt. Goalin reported in AIR. 1941 Patna 61 (FB), Azizul Huq Vs M/s. Hanif Ltd. and others, reported in 7 DLR, 287, Aswad Miah Vs. Shahidullah Miah, reported in 8 PLR (Dac) 1163, Samjan Kumar Dev Vs. Most, Halima Banu reported in 9 DLR (Dac) 213, Anil Das and others Vs. Mostaque Ahmed reported in 18 DLR 9 (Dac) 86, Mohammad Ismail and ors, Vs. Rahman and ors. reported in 53 CWN I.D.R. page 1, Messrs. Mamtaz Malick Vs. Taxing Officer, reported in 20 DLR (Dac) 599.

30. In all these cases attempts have been made to discover the real character of a District Judge or a Deputy Collector or some other functionary when they have been charged under some particular legislative enactment with the duty of taking certain decisions or making certain orders. An answer has been sought to be found to the question as to whether such a person was a Court or a persona designate from an analysis of their constitutions, functions and procedures they had to follow under the respective enactment.

31. Before we ourselves try to analyze the character of the District Judge functioning under sec. 39 of the Ordinance, we may with respect, refer to the following observation of FazI Ali, J. (as he then was) in the Full Bench case of Patna High Court referred to above:

"There is no real antithesis between the expressions "Persona designate and "Court"; in other words, even a persona designate may be a Court. Whether he is a Court or not depends upon his powers and the functions which he has to discharge."

<u>32. Although there is no exhaustive definition of a Court in any statute, a long line of judicial decisions of unquestioned authority have pointed out certain essential characteristics which invest a body with the character of a Court and have laid down certain tests which may distinguish it from a body which has some trappings of a Court but is not in fact, a Court.</u>

<u>A Court is, according to Coke on Little-ton, a place where justice is judicially administered and justice is understood, in the forensic world, to be a decision of a binding nature given on a point of dispute in a list between two or more contending parties by applying the law of the land to the facts of the case, untrammeled by the subjective attitude of the decision making body in exercise of the judicial power of the state and by following a judicial procedure.</u>

<u>33. In this connection we may refer to the view of Scott, C.J as given in Cooper Vs. Wilson and others as reported in 1937) L R 2 K B D. 309 about what a judicial decision is and how it can be distinguished from a quasi-judicial one:</u>

<u>"A true judicial decision presupposes an existing dispute between the two or more parties and then involves 4 requisites (i) the presentation (not necessarily orally) of their case by the parties to the dispute, (ii) if the dispute between them is a question of fact the ascertainment of the fact by means of evidence adduced by the parties to the dispute and often with the assistance or argument by or on behalf of the parties on the evidence, (iii) if the dispute between them is a question of law the submission of legal argument by the parties and (iv) a decision which disposes of the whole matter by a finding upon the facts in dispute and an application of the law of land to the facts so found including, where required, a ruling upon any disputed question of law. A quasi judicial decision equally presupposes an existing dispute between two or more parties and involves (i) and (ii) but does not necessarily involve (iii) and never invoices(iv)"</u>

<u>If would, however, be interesting to note that attempts have been made to lay down certain negative propositions for showing that the existence of certain characteristics, in spite of being ordinarily attributes of a Court, will not by themselves, make a body a Court and we may refer to the oft-quoted observation of Lord Sankey. L.C. made in the case of Shell Company of Australia Limited Vs, Federal Commissioner of Taxation as reported in L. R. 1931 A.C. 275.</u>

<u>"The authorities are clear to show that there are Tribunals with many of the trappings of a Court which, nevertheless are not Courts in the strict sense of exercising judicial power.</u>

<u>***************** ********************* *************</u>

<u>In that connection it may be useful to enumerate some negative propositions on this subject; (1) A tribunal is not necessarily a Court in this strict sense because it gives a final decision, (2) Nor because it hears witness on oath, (3) Nor because two or more contending parties appear before it between whom it has to decide, (4) Nor because it gives decisions which affect the rights of subjects, (5) Nor because there is an appeal to a Court, (6) Nor because it is a body to which matter is referred by another body."</u>

<u>These negative propositions, though helpful, are sometimes bewildering for the purpose of determining the basic character of a judicial tribunal. it has, therefore, been sometimes observed that although it is extremely difficult to say what a Court is but it is comparatively easy to say what a Court is not.</u>

34. Exercise of judicial power of the state, however, was considered to be the determining factor for in vesting a body with the character of a Court in the aforesaid case of Shell Company of Australia Ltd. Vs, Federal Commissioner and the Court of Review created under Federal Income Tax Assessment Act, 1922-25 of Australia was held not to be a Court exercising judicial power of the Commonwealth. In explaining what a judicial power is Lord Sankey, L.C. followed the definition given by Griffith, C.J. in Huddrat Parker Company Vs. Moorehead as reported in 8 C.L.R. 330 and held that it meant the power that every sovereign authority must of necessity have to decide controversies between the subjects or between itself and its subjects where the rights relate to life, liberty or property.

35. As pointed out by Chakraverty, J. (as the learned Judge then was) of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Khetsi Das Gongram Vs First Land Acquisition Collector of Calcutta reported in 50 CWN 758 same case AIR 1946 Cal 508 (S.B ) a Tribunal exercising judicial power or in other words, acting judicially does not mean merely that it is acting with fairness and impartiality on a proper consideration of all relevant materials after giving an opportunity to all contending par-ties to present their respective case. In order that exercise of judicial power or acting judicially may be a sign of acting as a Court, it must be acting as a part of the judicial machinery of the state, charged with the duty of determining the rights of one subject against another or a question of right between the subject and the state and discharging its function according to an established form of judicial procedure.

36. The Supreme Court of India has expressed itself in the similar way in the case of Bharat Bank Limited Vs. Employees of Bharat Bank Ltd., reported in AIR, 1950 (S.C.) 188 when, in analyzing the attributes of Courts of law, it has observed that they derive power from the state and are exercising the judicial powers of the state.

<u>37. If we now examine the provisions of section 39 of the Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan Ordinance in the light of the tests and criteria laid down in the aforesaid authorities we have no hesitation to hold that the District Judge in entertaining and deciding a matter under section 39 of the Ordinance acts as a Court of law.</u>

38. According to the provisions of section 39 an application under the said section shall have to be made to the District Judge within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the concern carries on its business. The jurisdiction referred to must necessarily be the jurisdiction of the District Judge as the presiding Judge of the principal Civil Court of original civil jurisdiction of District Judge as used in the said Ordinance but by subsequent amendment, for the purpose of extending the meaning of the words "District Judge" clause (ee) was inserted in section 2 which is to the following effect:—

"District Judge" shall include in respect of places where a District Judge does not have unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in original civil suits, a High Court Judge or a Bench of a High Court exercising original civil jurisdiction".

39. Section 3(17) of General Clauses Act, which will have application in the present case defines "District Judge" in the following manner:-

"District Judge" shall mean the Judge of a principal Civil Court of original civil jurisdiction but shall not include High Court in the exercise of its ordinary or extraordinary civil jurisdiction".

40. These definition may not be by themselves decisive in determining the character of the District Judge entertaining a proceeding under section 39 of the Ordinances as a Court of law but they are of some importance insofar as they point out that a District Judge who has been authorized to decide such a proceeding is the presiding Judge of a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction and functions as an important member of the ordinary judicial system of the country.

41. Powers have been conferred by the said provisions upon the District Judge to make certain orders affecting the rights of certain parties which are ordinarily, for their determination and enforcement, within the scope of general jurisdiction of the ordinary course of the Court. But in order to provide for making credits facilities expeditiously available to Industrial concerns and Industrial Development Bank was established under the provision of the said Ordinance. The said Bank would carry on and transact several kinds of business including advancing and lending of money and opening of cash credits for the specific purpose of assisting the industrial concerns upon security of several specific kinds of properties. Now if a certain industrial concern wants to avail itself of the facilities provided by such a Bank, it shall have to be liable to be sued before a District Judge for an order for the sale of its properties pledged mortgaged hypothecated or assigned to the Bank as security for the loan, or for transfer of the management of the concern to the Bank or for an injunction ad interim, in case of default or breach of any condition of any term in accordance with somewhat summary kind of procedure provided in section 39 of the Ordinance. An application which the Bank may chose to file on the ground of a breach of any condition of default made by the borrower concern shall have to be constituted in accordance with subsection (2) of the said section. Upon presentation of such an application certain ad-interim orders as prescribed in sub-section (3) or sub-section (4), as the case may be, shall have to be passed. At the time of the passing of the ad-interim orders under either of the aforesaid sub-sections notice shall have to be issued upon the borrower concern calling upon it to show cause why appropriate relief as prayed for should not be granted. If no cause is shown in pursuance of the aforesaid notice, the District Judge shall under sub-section (7) make forthwith the ad-interim order absolute and direct the sale of the attached properties or transfer the management of the Bank or confirm the injunction as the case may be. If, however, the cause is shown the District Judge shall proceed to investigate the claim of the Bank under subsection (8) and the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure shall, as far as practicable, apply to such proceedings After completing the inquiry under sub-section (8), the District Judge shall pass necessary orders as mentioned in sub-section (9) granting appropriate reliefs or refusing to grant suet reliefs Under sub-section (11), an appeal lies to the High Court against an order passed under subsection (7) or under sub-section (9) It is clear that the District Judge who is a part of the ordinary judicial system of the country becomes seized of a dispute under section 39 of the Ordering which arises out of an assertion of a legal right pertaining to enforcement of a security respecting repayment of a loan. Such a dispute can be litigated in the ordinary Courts of country in accordance with the ordinary judicial procedure. For the purpose of expeditious settlement of a claim and in order to avoid delay which is inevitable under the ordinary procedure, a special procedure has been devised in section 39 of the Ordinance. Nevertheless, the District Judge has to investigate the claim in accordance with the ordinary judicial procedure as provided in the Code of Civil Procedure and determine the dispute judicially by giving a binding decision in the case. The District Judge in disposing of the dispute has to finally determine the rights of parties pertaining to the dispute subject to the scrutiny of the High Court in an appeal, if so preferred. That the order passed by the District Judge for attachment and sale of the properties is a final determination of the rights of the parties of binding nature has been further made clear in sub section (10) which provides that an order for attachments and sale of the properties shall be carried into effect as far as may be in accordance with the provision of Code of Civil Procedure as if the Bank were a decree holder.

<u>42. On a consideration of the relevant provisions of the Ordinance, we find ourselves at one with the view that the District Judge in disposing of a proceeding under section 39 of the Ordinance is to set judicially and does exercise judicial power of the state and as such acts as the Court of the District Judge. We, therefore, do not find prima facie any substance in this plea of the learned Advocate for the borrower concern that the District Judge was a persona designer and not a Court So we hold that the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the plaintiff has not been able to make out prima facie case cannot be disturbed and that the learned Subordinate Judge was right in rejecting the prayer for temporary injunction.</u>

43. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, the learned Advocate for the creditor Bank has contended in support of the appeal No. 25 of 1971 that the learned Subordinate Judge having found that the plaintiff had not been able to make out a prima facie case and rejected the prayer for temporary injunction on the basis of said finding was wrong in giving direction that the mortgaged and hypothecated properties should be sold for realization of Rs. 3,66,491 .51 paisa only and the excess sale-proceeds should remain in the deposit of the Court, ending disposal of the suit. The learned Advocate has submitted that there is no basis for imposing such a condition. We think that there is substance in this contention of the learned Advocate. The plaintiff having failed to make out a prima facie case to the effect that the order of amendment dated 21-8-65 increasing the rate of interest was a nullity is not entitled to an order of the Court rendering the said order of amendment inoperative during the pendency of the suit.

44. In the result, the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 29 of 1971 is dismissed with costs and the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 25 of 1971 is allowed with costs and we set aside that part of the order which is to the effect that the mortgaged and hypothecated properties should be sold for the realization of Rs. 3, 66,491.51 only and the excess sale-proceed should remain in deposit in Court pending disposal of the suit. We assess a consolidated hearing fee for these two appeals at Rs. 1020/- The appeals having been disposed of, the connected rules stand discharged without any order as to costs.

M. Nurul Huda.—I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
Since the questions of law and facts involved in the aforesaid writ petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution are almost same, they were taken up together for hearing.

2. Rules in the aforesaid writ petitions were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the criminal proceedings pending before the respective Labour Courts under sections 307 read with section 310 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 should not be declared to have been initiated without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

3. In Writ Petition No. 8958 and 8960 of 20 I 0, both the respondent Nos. 2 filed the Bangladesh Labour Law (Criminal) Case No. 432 and 423 of 2010 before the First Labour Court, Dhaka under sections 307 and 310 of the Labour Act, 2006 (hereinafter called "the said Act") alleging, inter alia, that they joined the petitioners' establishment B 2 B Excellence Ltd. on (2-9-2006 and 1-3-2008 respectively without any appointment letters. While serving as Line QC under the Sewing Quality section, they were orally terminated on 22-4-2010 along with some other workers without any prior notice. Upon such termination, although their employers were obliged under law to pay Taka 44,004 and Taka 39,004 respectively on account of their arrear wages and termination benefits etc, they were paid nothing. They then initiated the impugned criminal proceedings, after serving a legal notice, on the allegations that the employer-petitioner, by such non-payment, violated the provisions under sections 3 and 123 of the said Act and, as such, liable to be punished under section 307 of the same.

4. In Writ Petition Nos. 4308 and 4309 of 2010. both the respondent Nos. 2 also filed Bangladesh Labour Law (Criminal) Case No. 121 of 2009 and 533 of 2008 before the First Labour Court, Dhaka under sections 307 and 3 10 of the said Act, alleging, inter alia, that they joined the establishment of the petitioners namely “দৈনিক যায়যায় দিন” on 1-4-2006 and 1-6-2006 as Assistant Editor and Translation Editor respectively. However, they were terminated from their services on 23-9-2008 and 29-6-2008 without any prior notice. Upon such terminations, they were entitled to receive Taka 3,88,622 and Taka 5,42,747 respectively as per the 7th Wage Board Decisions on account of termination and other benefits. However, they were paid only Taka 1,94,117 and Taka 2,28,391 respectively. Thus, they initiated the impugned proceedings, after serving Legal Notices, against the petitioners on the allegation that the petitioners had violated the provisions of the said Act.

5. The petitioners in Writ Petition No. 8958 and 8460 of 2010 obtained the aforesaid Rules after obtaining bail from the concerned Labour Court. The petitioners in Writ Petition Nos. 4308 and 4309 of2010 also obtained bail from the concerned Labour Court and challenged the impugned proceedings through the said writ petitions after the concerned Labour Court had rejected their applications for discharge.

6. The legal question involved in all the aforesaid Rules is same which is that whether or not the petitioner-employers are liable to be prosecuted for punishment under sections 307 read with section 310 of Labour Act, 2006 or under any other provisions for their alleged violation or non- compliance of the provisions of the said Act or Rules or Regulations or Scheme made there under without or before exhaustion of legal avenues as provided by section 33 and/or section 132 of the said Act.

7. At the very outset, the learned advocates for the petitioners have referred to two decisions of this Court, namely the cases of Sayeed Ahmed Chowdhury vs SM Zahidul Islam (Zahid), 63 DLR 212 (decided under criminal jurisdiction) and Kazi Rokanuddin Ahmed vs Labour Court, 63 DLR 382 (decided under writ jurisdiction) (hereinafter called "Sayeed Ahmed's case" and "Kazi Rokanuddin's case" respectively).

8. The cumulative submissions of both the learned Advocates (Mr Abdul Khaleque and Mr Syed Moyeenul Huq), appearing for the above mentioned two sets of petitioners respectively, are that since the dispute involves determination of facts, namely whether the concerned workers were at all terminated or not and as well as determination of actual monetary liability of the employers, the remedies available to the workers are either grievance proceedings under section 33 or proceedings under section i3,L, and under both the provisions, the Labour Court may resolve the disputes like a Civil Court. Thus, according to them, since the Labour Court, in exercise of criminal jurisdiction under section 307 or other relevant provisions of the said Act cannot be in a position to resolve those bonafide disputes involving civil liabilities of the employers, the impugned criminal proceedings should not be allowed to continue.

9. On the other hand, Mr Rajik-al-Jalil learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing with the leave of the Court, submits that the decisions in Sayeed Ahmed's case and Kazi Rokanuddin's case have not decided the questions of law involved in the matters in clear terms. According to him, section 307 criminal proceeding is an independent proceeding which is not in any way dependent on the exhaustion or initiation of the proceedings either under section 33 or section 132. He further submits that whether a worker will take recourse to section 33 or section 132 of the said Act is dependent on the desire of the concerned worker as both the provisions made it optional for the said worker, and if a particular worker does not intend to take recourse to those two provisions, he will not be rendered bereft of any remedy in so far as the penalty for violation of the provisions of law by the employers is concerned.

10. Heard the submissions and considered the materials on record. In view of section 30, once the employment of a worker has terminated due to his retirement, discharge, retrenchment, dismissal or termination etc, the appointing authority is obliged to pay his entire dues (প্রাপ্য সকল পাওনা) within thirty working days from such end of service. On the other hand, section 123 oblige the employers to pay the entire wages (প্রদেয় সকল মজুরী)of the concerned worker within seven working days from the end of his employment on account of retrenchment, discharge, removal, dismissed etc. Besides, in case of Wage Board Decision for the newspaper employees, section 148 made it mandatory for the employers to com- ply with the decisions of the Wage Board. It also recognized the rights of the newspaper employees/workers to receive minimum wages declared by the said Wage Board Decision. Section 149 even made it prohibitory for the employers to pay any wages below the rate determined by the Wage Board.

11. Now, the question is whether the legal obligations to pay as mentioned in sections 30, 123 and 148 and the prohibition under section 149, are mere literature in the statute book or they have any meaningful purpose. If we accept the submissions of the learned advocates for the petitioners, the said obligations as mentioned under sections 30, 123 and 148 and the prohibition under section 149 will be rendered to be mere letters in the statute book without any teeth to bite. Section 33 and 132 provides for civil remedies in accordance with certain procedures and limitation period through which the Labour Court has power to settle the dispute in exercise of its civil jurisdiction and may, in an appropriate case, direct the employer to even pay the entire dues or entire wages, as the case may be. Penalties for non-compliance of any such direction of the Labour Court have also been mentioned in the relevant provisions. These provisions are optional for the workers concerned. The issue is what if any person in this cases the employers, violates, or does not comply with, any specific provisions of the said Act, Rules, Regulations or Scheme there under. This aspect is dealt with by some specific penalty provisions enumerated from sections 283 to 306 under Chapter 19 of the said Act, and section 307 is there as a residue penalty provision. Section 307 runs as follows:

“৩০৭। অন্যান্য অপরাধের দন্ড। কোন ব্যক্তি এই আইন  বা কোন বিধি, প্রবিধান বা স্কীমের কোন বিধান লংঘন করিলে বা মানিতে ব্যর্থ হইলে এবং ইহার জন্য উহাতে অন্য কোন দন্ডের বিধান না থাকিলে, তিনি তিন মাস পর্যন্ত কারাদন্ডে, অথবা এক হাজার টাকা পর্যন্ত অর্থদন্ডে, অথবা উভয় দন্ডে দন্ডনীয় হইবেন”।

12. Upon reading the relevant Petition of Complaints as annexed to the aforesaid writ petitions, it appeals that the basic allegation of the concerned workers is that the employers concerned either violated the provisions of the said Act or did not comply with the specific provisions of law. Although in Writ Petition No. 4308 and 4309 of 2010 the Petition of Complaints alleged violation of sections 148 and 149 and specific penalty for such violation is provided under section 289, this non-mentioning of section 289 or wrong mentioning of section 307 should not in any way vitiate the entire proceedings initiated against the employer if it is found that the allegations made in the Petition of Complaints do disclose the culpability punishable under the said Act. Therefore, our prima-facie view is that the criminal proceedings concerned in the aforesaid writ petitions should not be nipped in the bud and they should be allowed to proceed. The Labour Court in those proceedings will of course not endeavour to determine exact liability and will not pass direction to pay like in the proceedings under sections 33 and 132. Nevertheless, it will go into the merit of liability just to determine the culpability as to whether there was any violation of, or non-compliance with, any provisions on the part of the employers. Any bonafide dispute, if raised by the employers, can also be taken care of in a criminal proceeding either at the time of framing of charge or subsequently. We find indirect support of our this view in an unreported judgment of our High Court Division dated 17-4-2002 in Writ Petition Nos. 2100-2111 of 1999.

13. Although the legal issues involved in the instant writ petitions were not elaborately discussed and/or answered in Sayeed Ahmed's case and Kazi Rokanuddin's case as referred to above, it is palpable that the basic ratio intended to be expressed by their Lordships in those cases is that no criminal proceedings can be initiated or proceeded against the employers under section 307 or any other provisions for the following reasons:

a)	no order of Labour Court was violated or non-complied with (Sayeed Ahmed's case);

b)	the concerned worker claimed some dues which involve calculation and, as such, a civil dispute (Sayeed Ahmed case);

c)	initiation of criminal proceedings under sections 307 and 310 is "a misconception of Law" as the concerned work failed to take prior recourse to grievance proceedings under section 33 (Kazi Rokanuddin 's case);

<u>14. Thus, it is very much understandable that, with all due respect to the Hon'ble Judges, we find it is very difficult to agree with the basic ratio as intended to be settled or expressed in the Sayeed Ahmed's case and Kazi Rokanuddin's case. Therefore, the instant writ petitions should be referred to the Hon'ble Chief justice for decision by a Full Bench as per the provisions of Chapter- VI, Rule-I of the High Court Division Rules. Accordingly, let the aforesaid Writ Petitions be placed before the Hon'ble Chief Justice for a decision by a Full Bench in view of Chapter-VII, Rule-l of the High Court Division Rules.</u>

HIGH COURT DIVISION

(Special Original Jurisdiction)

Md Nizamul Huq J

Quazi Reza-ul-Haque J

ABM Altaf Hossain J

Writ Petition Nos. 8958, 8960, 4308 and 4309 of 2010.

Mehreen Asaf and another ------ Petitioner

Vs.

Chairman, First Labour Court, Dhaka and another ------ Respondent

Judgment June 18th, 2013

Aminul Huq with Abdul Khaleq, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners.

Rajik-al-Jalil, DAG Sakila Rowshan, DAG with Sarmina Haque, Sarwardi Amatul Karim, AAG ----- For the State.

Khurshid Alam Khan, with AKM Nasim, Advocates ----- For Intervener, Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust.

Judgment

Md Nizamul Huq J: Since the questions of facts and law involved in the 4(four) aforesaid writ petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (The Constitution) are almost same and all these matters were heard together by a Division Bench of this Court presided over by Mr Justice Bazlur Rahman and Mr Justice Sheikh Hasan Arif and that Bench by order dated 13-1-2013, found it difficult to agree with the basic ratio as intended to be settled or expressed in the Sayeed Ahmed's case and Kazi Rokanuddin s case (reported in 63 DLR 212 decided under criminal jurisdiction and 63 DLR 382 decided under writ jurisdiction respectively), therefore the instant 4 writ petitions were referred to the Honorable Chief Justice for a decision by a full Bench as per provisions of Chapter VII, Rule 1 of the High Court Rules. Accordingly these 4(four) writ petitions were placed before the Honorable Chief Justice for reference to a full Bench and the Honorable Chief Justice has formed this full Bench to hear those 4(four) writ petitions.

16. Rules in the aforesaid writ petitions were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the criminal proceedings pending before the respective Labour Courts under sections 307 read with section 310 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 should not be declared to have been initiated without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

17. In writ petition No. 8958 of 2010 and 8960 of 2010, both the respondent No.2, were the complainants in Criminal Case No. 432 and Criminal Case No. 423 of 2010 filed before the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka under section 307 and 310 of the Labour Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the said act) alleging inter-alia that the complainant joined the petitioners establishment on 2- 9-2006 and 1-3-2008 respectively without any appointment letters; while serving in the sewing quality section they were orally terminated on 22- 4-2010 along with some other workers without any prior notice. Upon such termination although their employers were obliged under the law to pay Taka 44,004 and Taka 39,004 respectively on account of their arrear wages and termination benefits etc, they were paid nothing. They then initialed the impugned criminal proceedings after serving legal notice on the allegations that the employer-petitioner by such an act of non-payment violated the provisions under section 30 and 123(1) of the said act and, as such, liable to be punished under section 307 of the same.

18. In writ petition No. 4308 of 2010 and writ petition No. 4309 of 2010, both the complainant respondent Nos. 2 also filed Labour Court Criminal Case Nos. 121 of 2009 and 533 of 2008 before the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka under section 307 and 310 of the said act alleging inter-alia that they joined the establishment of the petitioners namely ‘Dainik Jai Jai Din’ (a daily newspaper) on 1-4-2006 and 1-6-2006 respectively as Assistant Editor and Translation Editor respectively. However, they were terminated from their services on 23-9-2008 and 29-06-2008 respectively without any prior notice. Upon such termination they were entitled to receive Taka 3,88,622 and Taka 5,42,747 respectively as per the 7th Wage Board Decisions on account of termination and other benefits. However, they were paid only Taka 1,94,117 and 2,28,391 respectively, thus they initiated the impugned proceedings after serving legal notices against the petitioners on the allegation that the petitioners had violated the provisions of the said act.

19. All the petitioners in writ petition No. 8958 of2010, writ petition No. 8960 of2010, writ petition No. 4308 of 2010, and writ petition No. 4309 of 2010 obtain the aforesaid Rules, after obtaining bail from the concerned Labour Court, challenging the impugned proceeding of the concerned Labour Court rejecting their application for discharge.

20. The legal question involved in all the aforesaid Rules are the same, as to whether the petitioner employers are liable to be prosecuted for punishment under sections 307 read with section 310 of Labour Act 2006 or under any other provisions for their alleged violation or non-compliance of the provisions of said Act, rules, or scheme made there under without or before exhaustion of legal avenues as provided by section 33 and or section 132 of the said Act.

21. It may be mentioned here that in Criminal Case No. 432 of 2010 there are two accused per- sons 1) Mehreen Asaf, Managing Director and 2) Col. (Retd) Mostafa Ali, Executive Director and in the writ petition only Mehreen Asaf is the petitioner and the accused Col. (Retd) Mostafa Ali is not a party. Similarly in Writ Petition No. 8960 of 2010, the said Mehreen Asaf is the petitioner and the another accused Col. (Retd) Mostafa Ali is not a petitioner. In writ petition No. 4308 of 2010, which relates to Criminal Case No. 121 of 2009, 5(five) accused persons are there and all of them are petitioners in the Writ Petition No. 4308 of 2010. In writ petition No. 4309 of 2010, challenging the legality of Criminal Case No. 533 of 2008, wherein 5(five) accused persons are there and all the 5(five) accused persons are petitioners.

22. Mr Aminul Haque with Mr Abdul Khaleque, the learned advocates appeared for the petitioners in the writ petitions, while Mr Rajik- al-Jalil, the learned Deputy Attorney-General with Ms Shakila Rowsan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, Ms. Sarmina Haque, Md Sarwardi and Ms AmatuI Karim AAGs appeared for the government. But none appeared for the accused respondent No.2 in all the cases. While the matter was being argued, Mr Khurshid Alam Khan the learned advocate appeared with a prayer on behalf of Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust to appear as intervener. The prayer was allowed and Mr Khurshid Alam Khan with Mr AKM Nasim, the learned advocates appeared for the intervener. All the petitioners in their writ petitions stated inter-alia that the claim of the respondent complainants are monetary claim, which is required to be determined and, as such, it does not constitute any criminal offence under section 307 of the said Act. The allegations of violation of section 30 and 123(1) of the Act is that if due salary, termination benefits etc. has not been paid to the complainant within the time stipulated in these sections that does not constitute any criminal offence because of the fact that there are specific provisions of settling the disputes under sections 33 and 123 of the said law. It was further contended that the dispute arose out of termination of services, so that is to be adjudicated under section 33 of the Bangladesh Labour Law, 2006 which contains inter-alia that:

23. It was further contended that non-compliance of section 123 of the said law is to be adjudicated under section 132. And as per section 132(5), the Court has power to give 25% compensation of the salary as fine, which is a punishment according to the section 53 of the Penal Code, and, as such, this proceeding under section 307 is illegal and is liable to be declared without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

It is further submitted that since the dispute involves determination of facts that is determination of actual monetary liability of the employers, the remedies available to the workers are either convene proceedings under section 33 of the Act, or to initiate proceedings under section 132 of the Act, and under both the provisions the Labour Court may resolve the disputes like a civil court. Thus since the Labour Court in exercise of criminal jurisdiction under section 307 or other relevant provisions of the said act cannot be in a position to resolve those disputes involving criminal liabilities of the employers, as such the criminal proceedings should not be allowed to continue.

It was also submitted that the intention of the legislature cannot be such that as soon as an employee is dismissed, retrenched, terminated or any dispute arose between the parties without trying to settle the dispute, anyone of the party will go to the Court by invoking its criminal jurisdiction, which will cause harassment to the other side. In the 4(four) cases referred herein upon which the writ petitions have been filed, according to them there was no settlement of the disputes and the complainant's side straight away went to the Labour Court invoking its criminal jurisdiction and arranged summons against the management, which cannot be the spirit and intention of the legislature. Moreover there are documents to show that the claim of the complaints after being correctly concluded has been given to the complainants and the complainants have received the said amount by giving written receipt as a full and final settlement of the claim by them and in a case like this, it cannot be the intention of the legislature to allow the complainant to go to the Court in its criminal jurisdiction to harass the other side.
